BasePK: 3718579

Speech:
Mr. Speaker, what has to be realized is that this is an important step in the resolution of
March 4, 1988

this important issue concerning the Lubicon Indian Band land claim. The setting up of this reserve and transfer of land by the province is an indication of the willingness of both Canada and Alberta to deal with the issue. What is important is that this transfer of land will be made without prejudice to the position of the parties involved. It does not affect the right of the band to seek additional reserve lands through negotiations or court action.
All we can say is that we are hopeful, this important step having been taken, we will be able to resolve the whole issue through negotiations.

BasePK: 3718614

Speech:
Mr. Speaker, an elemental rule of the House is that if Members want to put serious questions they should not misquote the people to whom they are referring. The Hon. Member has just misquoted me. He said that I made some kind of blanket representation regarding all the members of those organizations. I trust that he can read. Let him read the letter.
The letter says that some of the members of those organizations have been involved in or have counselled violence. That is the case.
I think it would be most unfortunate if a Member of Parliament of this House, for momentary celebrity or for partisan reasons, associated himself or herself with activities which encouraged or appeared to condone acts of violence.

BasePK: 3718620

Speech:
Mr. Speaker, this year's total personal tax package contains a 42-page tax guide with schedules, a 22-page information leaflet, 32 pages of additional forms, 10 pages of information circulars, as well as 34 interpretation bulletins. I also have a draft tax return for 1988 which Canadians will presumably fill out a year from now. When one adds the pages, it is actually greater than this year's form.
The Minister made a promise to the people of Canada that he would simplify the tax system and simplify the tax forms that Canadians would fill out. The tax return for next year will be more lengthy than this year's, which is eight pages compared to a single sheet in 1962. When will he keep the promise that he and his Government made to the people of Canada?

BasePK: 3718715

Speech:
Mr. Speaker, I also wish to present a petition signed by almost 100 Canadian citizens who are concerned about the free trade agreement which has been negotiated between the present Government and the United States.
The petitioners claim that the Government does not have the mandate to pursue the deal and that the negotiated agreement will hurt our sovereignty. As well, they are concerned about our autonomy in the energy sector. They believe that it would deny Canada the ability to devise our own economic future. They are also concerned that the agreement would have a negative effect on job growth in Canada.
They ask that Parliament be dissolved so that the Government could go to the people on this agreement.
I so move or I so introduce.

BasePK: 3718837

Speech:
Mr. Speaker, recently in a major article, the Toronto Star reported that individuals who belonged to the Khymer Rouge and participated in genocidal acts in Cambodia are residing in Canada as landed immigrants. This is a very serious allegation since the Khymer Rouge were responsible for two million innocent deaths, often using methods which rivalled the Nazis.
Such individuals have no right whatsoever to be allowed to live among civilized people. The Immigration Department and CSIS should immediately commence a full investigation to ascertain if the allegations are true. If it is found that indeed there are Khymer Rouge mass murderers in Canada, they should be charged with crimes against humanity. We must send out a strong message that there is no sanctuary in Canada, nor is there any clemency for this type of action against humanity.

BasePK: 3718840

Speech:
Mr. Speaker, on Friday, March 4, four citizens of Fort Albany, Ontario, a small isolated native community near James Bay, perished in a tragic fire. Delna Edwards, age 21, and her three sons, Kenny, Peter and Jeremy, all died, burned beyond recognition, because the community had no way to fight the fire other than with five-gallon pails. Our heartfelt sympathy goes out to the entire Fort Albany community.
This type of incident should not be occurring in native communities. Ste. Anne's School in the same community provides yet another example of a tragedy waiting to occur. It
March 7, 1988

took repeated warnings by fire inspectors before the Government took action to close the school. The children have now been without educational facilities for a month.
When will the Government realize that it has an obligation to take prompt action to guarantee that all Indian communities across the country are provided with the means to ensure that the safety of their people is not in constant jeopardy? The Government must re-examine its priorities and give Canadian native communities the attention and support they rightly deserve.

Oral Questions
The problems at Massey Ferguson have nothing to do with free trade. I have had an association with this company all of my life, and I knew something about it long before I was in government. I can tell Hon. Members right now that there has been free trade in farm machinery ever since I can remember. There are U.S. producers of farm machinery.
The problem in the farm machinery industry has to do with the protectionism that has been rising in the United States that has led to difficult times for farmers.

BasePK: 3719005

Speech:
Madam Speaker, I do not believe there is anyone in this House who disagrees with the main principle of this Bill, which is that Canadians, in terms of the Constitution of Canada, where there is significant demand, will be able to get services in the official language of their choice. I do not think there is any disagreement with that at all. But there is another principle contained in the Bill that in fact has nothing to do with official languages and has everything to do with constitutional changes as they affect the northern territories. I want to address this very briefly.
This principle is contained in Clause 90 of the Bill which states as follows:
The ordinance entitled the Official Languages Act, made on June 28, 1984
by the Commissioner in Council, as amended on June 26, 1986, may be
amended or repealed by the Commissioner in Council only if the amendment
or repeal is concurred in by Parliament through an amendment to this Act.
Of course, the Official Languages Act referred to here is the Official Languages Act of the Northwest Territories, a statute passed by the Legislative Assembly of the Northwest Territories.
The inclusion of this principle in the Bill is adding insult to the Meech Lake injury. It says in effect that the elected representatives of the people of the territories, at the provincial-type level, are not to be trusted, that Ottawa in some way has to maintain control, that the apron strings will remain tied.
There is no precedent in the Northwest Territories Act or any of the Acts establishing provinces where this type of control is to be maintained by the Parliament of Canada. In fact, in my opinion, and in the opinion of the people I represent, it is completely unnecessary and, coming as it does after the Meech Lake agreement in which the territories were treated so badly, it cannot fail to elicit this deep feeling on the part of my constituents.

March 7, 1988
Official Languages Act
If one examines the language laws in the Northwest Territories, one will find that we have probably the most progressive language law in the whole of Canada. Not only does the Act respect English and French as official languages, but it also respects the many indigenous languages spoken in the Territories which were spoken there probably thousands of years before ever a word of English or French was uttered on this continent. The people who speak those languages do not want to lose them. They are faithful to those languages. They feel the same way about their languages as the people in Quebec undoubtedly feel about the French language.
Much work has been done in the territories with respect to the extension of French language services to the small French speaking minority there. We would have to thank the Secretary of State of Canada (Mr. Crombie) for making funds available so that those services can be extended.
The history of Clause 90 goes back to the Joyal-Nerysoo Agreement of 1984. At that time Serge Joyal was the Secretary of State for Canada, and I suspect this was a rather unequal treaty. It is my suspicion that it was forced on Richard Nerysoo, who was then the Government Leader in the territories. It was done at a time when funds were to be made available to the territories for the provision of these French services as well as services in indigenous languages.
The agreement specified that Clause 90 as it now reads be applied to a Bill which was then entitled Bill C-25. It was the official languages Bill-not unlike the Bill we have before us today-which was to have been brought forward by the Liberal Government of the day but, for some reason or other, it died on the Order Paper.
Whatever the situation was in 1984, it certainly does not exist today. Clause 90 is redundant, superfluous and unnecessary. If for some remote reason, and I cannot foresee it happening, the territories wanted to amend their Official Languages Act in a way which took away the rights of Frenchspeaking people-and I do not think this would happen-there are various recourses available to the federal Government to deal with this situation. It is not necessary to put Clause 90 in the Bill. Federal authorities can instruct the Commissioner of the Territories to refuse consent to any amendment to the Official Languages Act of the Northwest Territories. Federal authorities retain the power of disallowance. It can disallow any territorial legislation. Over and above that, it has the power to enact overriding legislation should it so choose. Therefore, Clause 90 is not necessary at all.
On February 17, the Legislative Assembly of the Northwest Territories, feeling as strongly about this issue as I do, adopted the following resolution:
Whereas the people of the Northwest Territories and the Legislative Assembly of the Northwest Territories have in recent years taken large steps towards the achievement of responsible government;
And whereas there is presently, before the Parliament of Canada, a federal Bill which provides for a reduction in the legislative authority of the Legislative Assembly of the N.W.T.;
Therefore, be it resolved:
-that this Legislative Assembly declare its strong opposition, through the
Speaker, to the enactment of Clause 90 of Federal Bill C-72 presently before
the Parliament of Canada, which clause reduces the legislative authority of
this Assembly.
I would like to record my thanks to two Members of the House of Commons in particular who have spoken on this issue already. One, of course, is the Hon. Member for Cochrane- Superior (Mr. Penner) representing the Liberal Party who is in the House this afternoon. The other is the Hon. Member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Keeper) of the New Democratic Party.
Those of us who are familiar with northern issues realize that this is not a Party issue. Rather, it is one that acts against the interests of the territories eventually becoming a province in their own right. Hopefully, that is something that we are all agreed upon regardless of our Party pe [...truncated]

Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to be involved in this debate today. I would like to thank my colleagues who have spoken before me for the number of points they have made on this private Member's motion.
The motion is certainly one that, at first blush, all Hon. Members would find generally supportable. Upon further examination, however, I fear that the motion only covers one very small part of what is a major issue facing not only the environmental community but indeed all Canadians.
The motion calls for the Government to consider the advisability of intensifying research for alternatives to refrigerants such as freon which contain chlorofluorocarbons, CFCs, that erode the earth's ozone layer. Indeed, we have heard a number of Hon. Members speak, not only today but in past debates on this motion, and I think they have touched on many good points.
Obviously, whenever one jumps in or out of an air-conditioned vehicle or building, one does not stop to try to understand the way refrigerant coolants work. Certainly few people give serious enough consideration to the impact on the ozone layer and indeed the environment generally of the generically-named chlorofluorocarbons or CFCs.
In closing off this hour of debate tonight, I would like to paraphrase briefly a number of points my colleagues have
March 8, 1988

made. We heard of many of the major events that led up to the Vienna Convention for the protection of the ozone layer and the Montreal protocol. My colleague from London just now spoke eloquently of the role Canada has played in the development of these conventions and protocols and how we are working on international institutional mechanisms that will be in place on a global scale, as well as dealt with the domestic treatment of CFCs.
It has also been pointed out tonight that the need for scientific research is imperative. This need is probably exceeded only by the need for not only Canada but many of the countries of the world to recognize that shortsightedness and narrow self-interest will imperil all of us. The matter should be dealt with appropriately.
We recall the highlights of the conference co-sponsored by Environment Canada held in Washington in January. This conference was important because it identified concretely that there is a tremendous level of activity in the private sector to share research information and to initiate joint programs. As well, there is a sharing of information on current technologies designed to reduce CFCs and halons. Some of these initiatives include substitute chemicals, recycling, recovery and destruction.
The conference showed that producers, researchers, regulators, environmental groups and even the media are discussing the status of the development of product substitutes and alternative processes. Things are moving forward. A platform was also provided at the Washington conference for industry to report on its progress to date, a key element which goes to the heart of the motion that is before us today.
In debate, Hon. Members have talked about the unprecedented level of research that has been done. Research is moving forward on several fronts. We are clearly faced with an environmental problem caused by our ever-growing dependence on so-called halons and CFCs which are currently used in what many consider to be essential uses.
We have identified in a general way the Government's intention to address the obligations in the protocol arising from the Vienna Conference. Our Government has spoken very directly about continuing research efforts to find suitable alternative chemicals. We have pointed out that there are many hurdles remaining. We have discussed the products and the services, the technologies we now need to ensure that there is an orderly transition to more environmentally suitable products.
The Government has attempted to provide Hon. Members in this debate with a sense of our action plan and our timetable for meeting the mandated global reduction requirements for CFCs and halons. We have indicated that we are now doing several things. We are preparing for ratification of the Montreal protocol. We are preparing a comprehensive control options report. As well, we are collecting data to determine the cost benefits and the potential dislocations associated with each of the options to which I have referred. We have stated
Adjournment Debate
on numerous occasions that we need the Canadian environmental protection Act, not just to ratify the Montreal protocol but also to implement many of the control actions that will be taken.
In respect of the motion moved by the Hon. Member for Davenport (Mr. Caccia), the message of this Government is clear. There are many things that Government, industry, consumers and indeed all Canadians can and should be doing to remedy the ozone-depletion problem. Every participant in this issue should play a role to some extent.
Industry has an important responsibility, and I have mentioned thus far many of the actions internationally and domestically that the Government has taken. I want to end off this evening by touching briefly on the role of industry.
Because of the market-driven nature of this issue, we have seen the industry has what could only be called a foot race. This foot race involves the development and the technological advancement of alternatives to CFCs. In The Globe and Mail of February, just over a month ago, there was an article entitled "CFC replacement produced". It was a short piece which talked about the work of the Dupont chemical company in developing research in CFC alternatives at its New Jersey plant as well as in Canada.
While it is important that Government continue the work we are undertaking, I think this motion does not go far enough in saying what industry and indeed all Canadians can do.

This Bill represents the culmination of a legislative movement that has been fermenting and growing within the House of Commons and, indeed, within Canada for some time now. This movement has seen the introduction in the House of several Private Members' Bills dealing with the registration of lobbyists, principally, of course, presented by members of my Party, including one presented by our Party's spokesman for consumer and corporate affairs, the Hon. Member for Nickel Belt (Mr. Rodriguez).
Finally, the pressure of public opinion in respect of legislative initiative led the Government to realize that this was a matter of serious concern and import to a large number of Canadians. Consequently, in September of 1985, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney), in the context of a fairly wide-ranging statement on public-sector ethics, announced the Government's intention to have lobbyists registered. I think it is well worth the time to excerpt some of the statements the Prime Minister made in that open letter.
March 14, 1988

Along with instructions to Ministers on the hiring of family members, the conflict of interest post-employment code for public office holders and the experimental program of parliamentary scrutiny of Governor in Council appointments, on which the jury is still out since we have only had limited experience of it, the Prime Minister included as point five of his open letter the registration of lobbying activity. In expanding on that theme, he stated that we will require, among other things, paid lobbyists to register and identify their clients.
Within the life of the Government there has certainly been bad publicity surrounding the activities of lobbyists. Elowever, let us not forget that in previous Liberal Governments similar activity took place, attracting similar publicity, and justly so, because there were often cases where it was felt that people, for hire or for reward, had undertaken a key role in influencing legislation, its design or structuring programs, their drafting and implementation, and even the timing of regulations in some cases.
My Party is in broad agreement with the legislation the Government has introduced in Bill C-82. We are glad that the time has finally come when Canada will have a regime of registration of lobbyists that will allow Canadians comparable access to the sort of information that our cousins in the U.S. have had for many years; that is, information on who is trying to influence the Government, who is drawing a salary, remuneration or reward for their activities in trying to influence the process of Government, and who is buying the services of these lobbyists. They are known as lobbyists because of the tradition that they operate within the lobbies of this very Chamber. We will know who is paying them and what are their objectives.
First and foremost I think we should say that our Party is quite dubious about the value of the Tier I and Tier II formats that this Bill establishes. We would like to see all lobbyists disgorge the sort of information being demanded from Tier I lobbyists, who we might see as the full-time professional, freelance lobbyists, those who are always up for hire, so to speak, for sale to the highest bidder, compared with the Tier II lobbyists who are largely those instructed by their employers, professional associations, corporate business and trade associations, to seek not only specific legislative initiatives but also to broadly influence the climate of opinion, the focus of debate, the movement and interplay of ideas within Government and Parliament. Some of those lobbyists would have the facility, indeed, in some cases to be more influential than those who move from client to client or who, like many of the leading lobbying firms, have a number of clients on retainer and draw specific fees for specific assignments. Canadians are entitled to know who is doing what, who they are doing it for, who they are talking to, and how much money is changing hands on account of this lobbying.
Lobbying, of course, is a practice which has always been carried on, but in recent years it has become professionalized,

commercialized, and much more organized as well as much more recognized. Some 40 or 50 years ago people might undertake to act for some nominal recognition or compensation by way of intermediary in an age when communications were much less developed. When contact on a direct basis with a Member of Parliament or a member of the Government was certainly much more difficult than it is now, people might undertake to meet the Minister or Member of Parliament or even the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) within the lobby of the House and raise the concern of an individual or the legislative request of a group or body. Now, despite the fact that it is surely easier than it ever has been for the ordinary citizen, company, trade union or association, provincial Government or professional agency to contact members of the Government or organizations within our Parliament, we have this professionalization, and perhaps that is a word I am using a little loosely, but certainly this commercialization of the lobbying process which seems to have no end to it, which seems to be continually growing.
It was alleged back in 1985, and this may have something to do with the introduction of this legislation, that a company which has already been named here accepted a commission of some $2,000 to arrange a meeting between a fisherman and the then Minister of Fisheries and Oceans. This is an example, surely, of the type of lobbying which really should be eliminated, along with a recognition that there are indeed legitimate types of lobbying and very legitimate lobbying objectives.

Madam Speaker, first, the kind of industries we would like to see in the future include the high tech sector. The kind of future industries I am looking for for Vancouver Island are those which take advantage of rapid transportation by air that will not be expensive in weight and volume. On that basis, one of our fundamental economic needs is to preserve the environment of Vancouver Island as a good place for people to live and, therefore, as a good place for industries to locate.
With regard to the money that has already been spent, let us look at three expenses the Government took out of the $1.2 billion last year before the fund got fully operational. First was $79 million over five years for South Moresby Park. Members on all sides of the House supported the creation of South Moresby Park. But should that money necessarily have come out of the Western Diversification Fund?
Second, there was $9.5 million for shakes and shingles market development. The shakes and shingles economy of British Columbia was hit by the 35 per cent tariff imposed by our friends in the United States. In co-operation with the shakes and shingles manufacturers, the Western Diversification Fund is putting $9.5 million trying to expand that market again and perhaps find other markets.
What about the $53 million for the salmon enhancement project? It is this program that I want to question because that $53 million will be spent over the next five years. It will be added to $154.3 million spread over five years, money that will come from the Department of Fisheries and Oceans.
As you know, Madam Speaker, the Salmonoid Enhancement Program has been the responsibility of the Department of Fisheries and Oceans. During this last year the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. Siddon) went to the Cabinet Committee on Economic and Regional Development to tap into the policy reserve funds to the tune of some $50 million per year for the next five years. He was not given that money from the policy reserve fund from where it should have come. Instead, money was made available from the Western Diversification Fund. It is less money than the Minister was seeking, and it is just enough to barely maintain the current project levels. It is important funding.
The Salmonoid Enhancement Program is important to British Columbia. But is there some kind of a hoax being perpetrated on us? This money should have come from the regular Estimates of the Department of Fisheries and Oceans or from policy reserve funds. Instead, the Government makes a great show of announcing extra funding. It is called new money from the Western Diversification Fund but it is going back into what should have come from a line department. This use of the Western Diversification Fund to meet commitments that should be made from other departments, is, I think, a hoax.
While we support the concept and the principle of this Bill, we have to ask whether or not the Government is really committed. It seems the Government is not prepared to put its money where its mouth is in this whole area.

Mr. Speaker, I want to take this opportunity to pay a last tribute to a great Canadian, the Hon. Marcel Crete, Chief Justice of the Quebec Court of Appeal, who died Friday night in Montreal. We were very sad at the news of his death. Judge Crete contributed greatly to the development of law in Quebec.
Born in La Tuque, the Chief Justice went to school in Grand-Mere and Trois-Rivieres before going to Laval University. He was called to the bar in 1937 and studied at Osgoode Hall in Toronto.
The Chief Justice practised law in Grand-Mere for 29 years before being appointed to the Superior Court of Trois-Rivieres in September 1966. He was subsequently appointed to the highest court in the province, the Quebec Court of Appeal, in January 1972. Finally, in 1980 he became Chief Justice.
Respected by his colleagues and friends, Judge Marcel Crete was a man of integrity and principle. In 1986, he was awarded the Medaille du Barreau in recognition of his great legal skills and commitment to the community.

March 14, 1988
The death of Chief Justic Marcel Crete is a great loss to us all. I am sure my colleagues in the House share my grief and will want to join me in extending our sincere condolences to his family and friends.

If I may, Mr. Speaker, I should like first of all to point out to the Hon. Member that the remission order granted to the Goodyear Tire Company is worth $25 million over a four-year period, and not $50 million as he has

March 15, 1988
Adjournment Debate
just stated. I should like also to emphasize that these $25 million are not a subsidy, but a remission on duties otherwise payable on this company's future imports.
Mr. Speaker, I am sure the Hon. Member is aware that the Canadian tire industry is making a major contribution to the economy of this country, with a production worth up to $1.7 billion in 1985. Tire manufacturing in Canada provide jobs to some 11,000 people, including 4,300 in Ontario, 4,000 in Nova Scotia, and 2,700 in Quebec. This industry has been exposed to strong restructuring pressures, to a series of takeovers, mergers and acquisitions which have resulted in a significant number of job lossses. Moreover, in anticipation of free trade with the United States, it is important, not to say essential, that the Canadian tire industry should become completely competitive on the North American market.
A remission is considered as a proper mechanism to encourage new investments in Canadian tire manufacturing firms and thus ensure the future of that industry in Canada. More specifically, the purpose of this remission of duty is to help tire makers streamline their facilities and rationalize their North American operations. Moreover, the tire duty remission program will avert future job losses and, as you know, will preserve existing jobs in this industry.
Clearly, if tire makers do not meet the expectations both of the Government and the industry, it will be the Government's responsibility to put an end to these benefits.
The Government is quite concerned about the effects of manpower upheaval and disruption from lay-offs. However, we should not loose sight of the jobs which will be secured as a result to the steps taken by the Government. I understand that only a few workers have been laid off and could still be recalled following the closing of the Goodyear plant in Toronto. I understand also that Goodyear has set up an employment priority program in Valleyfield and Medicine Hat. I know that the company has offered the same transfer rights to any new plant which could be built within the next five years, provided such employees meet the hiring requirements.
I have also been advised that Goodyear not only has met all of its legal commitments, but exceeded its obligations under the agreement it signed with its employees, when it ended its operations.
Mr. Speaker, our Government feels that the tire duty remission program will help tire manufacturers become more efficient. It is quite concerned about the long term profitability of Canadian tire manufacturers and we believe that the steps we have taken will open for them interesting opportunities in the future.

The ascension of Queen Elizabeth II to the Throne is a day that is very fresh in my memory. Her father, the late King George VI, died on my sixth birthday. Thus, since my sixth birthday, both in Great Britain and here in Canada, I have only known Queen Elizabeth II as the reigning monarch. Therefore, I think it fair to say that my formative years, my maturing years, and the years of my adulthood and political career have been spent under the reign of Queen Elizabeth II.
She has surely seen some changes in those 36 years. After all, in 1952 when she acceded to the Throne, the Commonwealth was by and large made up of colonies which were in some form of tutelage or subordinate relationship to Great Britain under the British Crown.
Now I believe that we can truly say that the Commonwealth is a commonwealth of nations where all, despite differences in size, prosperity, and influence within world society, are rightly and correctly treated as being equal within the framework of the Commonwealth.
The Commonwealth has not been an institution merely for the preservation, the spread, or even the development of British culture. It has become a forum where nations that share a common heritage, particularly in terms of their institutions as well as the English language, can discuss matters of world affairs and can, when the spirit moves them, exercise collective influence on those world affairs.

It has not been the practice in Britain, although it is in some countries, to erect statues during the lifetime of the person commemorated or represented by the statue. It is still not something about which many of us who have British heritage feel particularly comfortable.

I do not feel it demeans or derogates in any way from Her Majesty the Queen and Her achievements to discuss that in the context of this motion. Noting the range of subjects which the motion has grouped together you will not be surprised, Mr. Speaker, that some specific areas will be discussed by other speakers for the Government today.
To begin with, let us be clear about the Canadian consumers referred to in the motion. Contrary to the impression which the Hon. Member tried to leave, they are not some special interest group with particular interests separate from those of everyone else. All Canadians are consumers. More to the point, their present and future well-being as consumers depends directly on the ability of the Canadian economy to produce new jobs and to produce higher incomes and new economic opportunities now and in the years ahead. Consumers are not only people dealt with by the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs but are consumers in the wider sense which I just mentioned.
The kind of negative thinking which is reflected in the motion before us today was soundly rejected by Canadians in September, 1984. Instead of approaching government this way they wanted a positive new approach to the economic challenges facing Canada. That is exactly what the Government has provided. We did not do this in an ad hoc way. We made clear to the Canadian people how we were going to proceed. We laid it out clearly in the agenda for economic renewal in
1984.	It is there for everyone to see.
Often governmental statements of that nature under Liberal Governments did not mean anything, they were mere cream puffs with very little substance and certainly not followed through seriously by the Government. In this case the agenda for economic renewal is truly a blueprint. The governmental engineers have gone to work with it and have built an edifice which is very impressive. We have stuck to our program, and the results more than bear out the success of our policies. In every instance the consumer wins.
As an example of how the consumer wins, in 1987 real growth in gross domestic product reached 3.9 per cent, a growth rate higher than that of the United States. That was the third consecutive year in which growth was in that range. That is a tremendous performance.
Interest rates, too, have been stable at three to four percentage points below the levels reached in September, 1984. The Hon. Member for Ottawa Centre (Mr. Cassidy) reminded the Hon. Member for Cape Breton-East Richmond (Mr. Dingwall) of this. Interest rates are much lower today than they were in September, 1984. Real interest rates are also down substantially in the same period, to the benefit of the Canadian economy as a whole and of Canadians in their role as consumers. Nothing is more difficult for consumers to cope with than high interest rates, and we have brought them down.
The typical five-year mortgage rate is a good example. It is now 11 per cent down from 14.25 per cent in 1984. What could be more relevant to a consumer than that? This represents a saving of $1,400 per year on a $50,000 mortgage amortized over 25 years. Is the Hon. Member against that kind of action on behalf of the consumer? Consumers are also homeowners. Houses needed to be built so that they can have a choice. Housing starts are up from 135,000 in 1984 to 246,000 last year, which is the highest annual level for housing starts since 1977. Nothing could be more important to consumers than that figure.
Of course, consumers must be employed. The unemployment rate is down to 8.9 per cent in 1987 from 11.3 per cent in 1984 when we took over from the Hon. Member's Party as Government. It was down even further, to 7.8 per cent in February of this year. In response to the interjection by the Hon. Member for Ottawa Centre, the unemployment rate is down in all provinces, which is good news for Newfoundlanders as well as people from all other provinces.
The decline in the unemployment rate reflects a tremendous achievement in job creation. February is the seventeenth consecutive month in which full-time employment increased. Since September, 1984, 1.213 million jobs have been created. That is what we have accomplished for Canadian consumers.
The growth in our gross domestic product in recent years has put us in the top rank of leading industrialized nations. In fact, people who study Canada are impressed with what they see. The latest survey of business investment intentions is a good example. While such news may not make the front page, it is astonishing that Canadian business is planning to increase its investment in plant and equipment by an extraordinary 17.3 per cent this year. Usually increased investment intentions are up by 2 per cent or 3 per cent, if at all, over the previous year. This is the largest real increase in private sector investment spending in nine years. We have achieved those results because we took the necessary action to ensure a positive environment for job creating growth and investment.
We have made substantial progress in deficit reduction and controlling the growth of the debt, thereby reducing the burden on the consumer who must ultimately pay the bills.

The NDP often tells us that we should increase government spending for one reason or another. However, we hear very little about how they would raise the revenue to do it.

Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to rise to speak on Bill C-52. It is the coastal trade Act which is designed to encourage growth in the Canadian coasting trade and create new opportunities for this industry and offshore exploration and development. It completely removes the coasting trade provisions from the Canada Shipping Act and incorporates amendments to them into the new Coasting Trade and Commercial Marine Activities Act. We are certain this new Act will give impetus to the marine tourism and shipbuilding industries. It will also create more jobs for seamen working in areas to be reserved for Canadians. These areas include commercial activities related to the exploration, development or production of mineral resources right up to the continental shelf.
Before I highlight some of the amendments adopted by our committee, I would like to take this opportunity to congratulate the Members on their hard work. I believe Members put aside their political interests in favour of determining the best policy for our country. Members examined this Bill with vigour. We spent more than 10 days in committee hearings. Members heard from 23 witnesses and questioned in depth all aspects and implications of the Bill. I believe the Bill provides an appropriate balance among the various Canadian interests and reserves, to the degree possible, Canadian jobs for Canadians.
The committee recommended, and the Government accepted, certain amendments to the original draft Bill, four of which I would like to highlight for the Members here today.
First, the deletion of the exemption for hydrocarbon production platforms will require a licence to be obtained before a foreign production platform can be used in Canada. This means that a search will be made to determine if a suitable Canadian production platform is available before the licence is issued, and only if no such Canadian platform is available will it be issued. I believe, Mr. Speaker, that this amendment will encourage Canadians to build platforms in

March 25, 1988
Coasting Trade and Commercial Marine Activities Act
Canada thereby providing job opportunities and encouragement to our shipbuilding industry.
Second, foreign cargo ships wishing to do business in Canada must obtain a temporary coasting trade licence and give 14 days notice of the proposed activity. This will allow Canadian shipping companies to adjust their schedules to allow as many Canadian vessels as possible to be employed. I would draw to Members' attention Clause 6(2) where the Governor in Council may make regulations prescribing special circumstances to be taken into account by the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. MacKay) for the purpose of subsection (1).
Third, Canadian cruise ships operating domestically in the trades using vessels with up to 250 overnight passenger accommodations are protected by this Bill. Members will recall that the first draft of the Bill had a 100 passenger limit. So-called foreign international cruise ships with much larger accommodation are encouraged to continue calling at Canadian ports and are exempt from this Bill.
Fourth, a provision has been inserted in the Bill permitting the Governor in Council to place a cap on the number of licences that may be issued. This provision is available to the Government in situations where it is in the public interest to do so.
Over-all, Mr. Speaker, the Bill enables the Canadian supply boat fleet to extend its range beyond the territorial sea to the outer edge of the continental shelf or 200 miles, whichever is the greatest. This area will be reserved for Canadian ships.
A waiver system that allows foreign flagships to enter the Canadian coasting trade and the offshore area when no suitable Canadian ship is available will remain. Since 99 per cent of the Canadian coasting trade is carried in Canadian ships, this is not expected to have much effect on the industry.
Exemptions to the legislation include fishing vessels, ships engaged in ocean research, including those operated or sponsored by foreign Governments, and ships assisting others in distress. These foreign vessels are controlled by other Canadian legislation or by international agreements. The Bill will also remove the historic anomaly in Canadian legislation that refers to British ships rather than Canadian ships. Currently, only three British ships remain in the coasting trade in Canada. It should also be noted that the thrust of the Bill is supported by Canada's provinces as well as many segments of the marine industry.
This Bill has been needed and has been in the mill for well over 20 years and I believe Members of Parliament will serve Canada well by its passage today.

Madam Speaker, I would first like to congratulate the Hon. Member for Laurier (M. Berger) and wish him a happy birthday.

In respect of some of the questions the Hon. Member has posed during the course of his speech, he wonders whether I had suggested that a national mission should mean that we do not continue to encourage the development of science and technology in other areas.
I do not want to have what I have suggested misunderstood. I think we have to look back on good examples of national missions of the past to get a measure of where, in the context of our over-all research and development thrust, this should be placed.
For example, let us consider the declaration of a national mission by President Kennedy to make the United States first in space. This meant the mobilization of abundant resources and the co-operation across a broad spectrum of American industry, academia and government laboratories in order to accomplish this mission, which was the dominant mission in the United States. This did not come at a cost to the rest of the research and development thrust in the United States. Indeed, at the same time there was a tremendous increase in resources being made available in the United States to all aspects of science, as well as to more research funding and to better quality teaching of science in universities and high schools.
A national mission is quite different from an area of emphasis. There is any number of areas on which we can have some emphasis. There are certainly possibilities for smaller, more narrowly defined missions. But none can take the measure of the type of national mission that is conceived of in this proposition. It challenges the imagination with respect to what it is capable of doing. It will generate new science, new industry and new engineering.
Let me point out that in developing export forms of hydrogen technology we can even look to photosynthesis, which is the biological process of primacy from which under natural conditions hydrogen really is the first product. We can talk about translating biology into engineering, to use sunlight directly to generate hydrogen. There is fantastic scope to this type of mission.
To compare this with the contribution of Canada to the space platform is to compare apples to oranges. There is no possible way that our involvement there can have the industrial and technological pay-off, diffusion of new technologies and the saleable products that this type of mission would generate.
I agree with the Hon. Member, we must continue in the broad scope of all the deficiencies that exist in Canada with respect to our standing internationally in science and research and development and we cannot let those other areas go. This
is the type of mission that is not completely predictable in what it will require. We must have an abundant storehouse of knowledge, skills and education in the sciences and engineering right across the board to make this mission work.
Industry needs to do its job in developing its technology. This is an area in which the involvement of Government in providing leadership is necessary. It is also necessary that Government make a contribution to the expenditures that will not yield an immediate pay-off to industry and which therefore will not draw the type of investment during the early years in many areas that will be necessary in the long term to develop.

With the company in private hands, as it is now as a result of the action of the Conservative Government, there is less government control of that. Whether research and development occurs in Canada, in the United States, or at all, in relation to this propeller technology aircraft at de Havilland, no longer depends on the Government of Canada. It has given up the right to control that, because it is no longer the shareholder and it no longer appoints the directors of the company. That is one example of a consequence of privatization. However, I hope that the Government is calling on de Havilland, under the contract of purchase and sale which does give some rights to the federal Government and some continuing responsibilities, to assure that a high level of research and development does occur in Canada.
I can tell the Hon. Member that I have recently attended at the plant at de Havilland, and in the next few weeks a number of Members of Parliament elected in the area of the plant will be there. The amount of research and development that goes

on there is impressive. One hopes that it will continue and, if possible, will increase.
On the other hand, the new element introduced into de Havilland that I support, but that I admit might be controversial, is that it is beginning to do more assembly and fabrication of other aircraft than those it is making from beginning to end in the plant. I consider that to be a good insurance policy for the corporation. After all, a one-product company is as vulnerable as that product. While de Havilland's current plane is a very big winner or a very big success, in due course it will start to become obsolete. I hope that that is a long way down the road, but when that time comes I think the union and the Member of Parliament representing the area, myself, will be very happy that the company has other lines of activity which provide high paying jobs for very highly trained people who work in the plant.
I am not sorry that it has gone into the assembly business to the extent that it has, and I am not sorry that it is more than just a one-product plant. However, there is something discouraging, I must say, about making parts which fit into somebody else's aerospace vision or into planes being designed, assembled, and flown out of other factories than the ones de Havilland has in Canada.
I remember visiting other aircraft plants in that area of Toronto which were making tail assemblies, for example. That was the whole thing the company was about or the plant was involved in. One had to be somewhat saddened that the Canadian aerospace industry had the type of truncation that it would not be doing something where creative energy or vision or research and development could enhance what it was doing. Mr. Speaker, like other Members of the House and other Canadians, I have concerns for the situation in which the Turks who arrived in Canada to claim refugee status, ultimately without success, find themselves.
Last Friday evening I went to meet the group of marchers to explain the Government's position to them. I met them collectively and individually so that they would have an opportunity to ask any questions.
Today I met with their leaders again to explain directly to them my position at this moment and to reiterate once again that our Immigration Act must be respected.

I repeat, Mr. Speaker that last Friday I went to meet the group of marchers, and today I met them again to explain directly my position and to reiterate that the Immigration Act must be respected.

As Hon. Members in the House know, Canada's Immigration Act provides us with a legal process to assess claims to refugee status that are made in Canada. The process allows for various levels of appeal, all of which have been tried and exhausted by these people.
We recognize that these Turkish citizens were originally the victims of unscrupulous travel consultants, but once in Canada they have taken every opportunity to exercise their appeal rights under due process of the law. Those who remained chose to continue with the process.
The prevention of this kind of unfortunate situation is one of the reasons we have been attempting to introduce new legislation in the form of Bill C-55 and Bill C-84. Bill C-55 will allow the Government to deal more quickly with refugee claims and thus reduce the incidents of people remaining in Canada while their claims are under review, sometimes for many months or years.
We recognize that this is a stressful time and a difficult time, but we must also remember that in reality these people are hopeful immigrants and not refugees. If we allow our system to be abused, those who are in genuine fear of their lives and need our protection will be at risk.

If these people leave voluntarily and respect our laws, once they are in Turkey they can go through regular channels and make a new application for entry into Canada.
As the Minister responsible, I will not hold the deportation order against them. If they satisfy the selection criteria for Canada and Quebec, they will be accepted.
As I said before, these people have had the benefit of due process. They have made use of the various provisions and guarantees available under our legislation. Their claims for refugee status were examined thoroughly and rejected by the Refugee Status Advisory Committee, by the Immigration Appeal Board, and, for those who decided to take their case even further, by the Federal Court of Canada. At each level, their claim for refugee status was denied.

Under Canada's immigration law, due process is a lengthy process. Complying with removal orders is the last step in the process for these people. I should also point out that some 400 of their compatriots have already chosen to return to Turkey of their own volition.
In considering the situation of these Turks, I am also mindful that today there are some 48,000 persons in Canada claiming refugee status, more people than live in a city in Canada such as Rimouski. Each of these persons also has a story to tell and they, too, must receive our attention and our fairness. Canada has a record of fairness. It has a record of compassion in the treatment of real refugees. It is important to examine this situation in the light of our broader efforts on behalf of refugees.
In 1987, 17,000 refugees were resettled from abroad, 12,000 came from government sponsorships and 5,000, I am pleased to say, were sponsored by private groups who are showing a growing interest in helping real refugees. In 1988, this Government has increased its sponsorship to 13,000 and we expect that private groups will continue to expand their sponsorship this year to some 6,000. It is interesting to note that in 1987, 8,165 of the sponsored refugees were women. Canada contributes millions of dollars annually, in addition, to refugee assistance abroad.

Canada provides every protection for genuine refugees arriving at its borders. Despite its record, the Government realized that its current method of processing refugee claims was inefficient.
Bill C-55 was introduced to provide for a more efficient, entirely equitable and faster process for refugee status recognition.
Madam Speaker, the issue today is those people who were ordered to leave Canada on the weekend and who decided not to obey that order. I stand behind this commitment. I wrote to the Turks to ask for their co-operation and compliance with the laws of Canada.
April 12, 1988

Mr. Speaker, for the fourth time since last summer I take the floor to speak about those forgotten Canadians who work for the minimum wage. They are so forgotten that Statistics Canada and the Department of Labour do not know how many under federal jurisdiction are living on the minimum wage. It is an indication of how minimal is the interest in the minimum wage.

April 18, 1988
Adjournment Debate
Their lot is hard enough in most provinces but harder still in industries under federal jurisdiction such as railways, airlines, shipping companies, radio stations, television channels, and telecommunications. It is harder because in so many instances-indeed in all but one-the federal rate is lower.
The hardship they endure, however, is due not only to the wage being so low-$4 per hour-it is due also in the way inflation is outstripping their wages. These are wages which are earned by low paid, unskilled, unorganized, and largely forgotten workers.
The last federal minimum wage increase was in May, 1986, almost two years ago. Since that time the Consumer Price Index has gone up over 8 per cent so that the $4 per hour of 1986 are now worth only $3.84 in 1988. It was little enough in 1986, impossibly low in 1988.
It is time, and over time, that this wage rate were reviewed and improved. I submit, as I did in raising this subject, that the solution must include not only raising the federal minimum wage but indexing it according to the Consumer Price Index.
That is done, is it not, Mr. Speaker, for old age security pensions? It is done for Canada pensions. It is done for public service pensions. It is done for parliamentary pensions. Why is it so impossible for us to consider doing the same for those who need it most?
This proposal is not any wildcat radical notion. It has been practised in France since 1952. It was recommended in the United States by the Minimum Wage Study Commission and the General Accounting Office in 1983. It is not an irresponsible notion that surfaces in Private Members' Hour or in the Adjournment Debate. It is demonstrably a reasonable proposal put forward and practised by major Governments.
I am aware that some economists argue against minimum wages at all. I submit that that is not the issue. To raise the point at all is really to be irrelevant. The fact is we have the minimum wage. We have it in every jurisdiction in Canada, federally, provincially, and territorially.
The issue becomes: Is the minimum wage adequate to the need. Is it keeping pace with the cost of living? Is it providing protection to those who need it most, those who do not have other advocacy than this Parliament can afford? I am speaking about people who do not have any trade unions to speak for them or any hired agents, high-priced lawyers negotiating contracts for them. These are people who have to look to where I am speaking. They have to look to Parliament. They have to look to the House of Commons to bring before the representatives of the people of Canada, and through them the people themselves, the need of those who are otherwise without a voice.
I think of people who are struggling to make do on this kind of minimum wage, not only those who receive it under the federal jurisdiction but those who receive it in provincial and territorial industries. I am impressed at how impossible their plight is, especially when I think of what it costs to put a roof
over one's head, the roof of just one rented room, or perhaps two or three rooms in a basement apartment in the riding of Scarborough West or some other part of Metro Toronto.
I see why we have the arrival and the apparent though tragic permanency of food banks, for housing today is costing such a percentage of anyone's income that when a person's income is minimal the result is impossible without supplementary assistance.
I ask the Government to expedite its consideration of this matter and, if possible, to take the second step of indexing this wage so that in the future workers will not have to wait until officials get around to considering them, but like Members of Parliament, like pensioners, they will automatically receive their just due.

Then we would have had a Canadian or North American vehicle that perhaps would have cost less. This opportunity has now been lost. Actually Lavalin Inc. of Montreal owns 85 per cent of UTDC, and the balance is owned by the provincial Government of Ontario. The trucks are now going to be built in Ontario. It is my view that every contract let by the Government of Canada should consider regional disparities, and the guidelines should be so amended. This contract was let in Ontario where there is buoyancy in the economy, whereas in both the West and the Maritimes unemployment is rampant and both need industries that will be there for a long time. We missed this opportunity to secure an industry in the West that would have provided a great deal of diversification for many years to come.

Basin up near your area. We are very proud of those skiing areas.

I would like to see this Bill go to committee where the Minister can appear along with other witnesses to discuss how we can maintain some of these excellent skiing facilities in order to bring tourists and other visitors to our parks so they can enjoy the facilities.

Mr. Speaker, the chief, the council, and the Spallumcheen Indian Band members reject the Minister of Indian Affairs' (Mr. McKnight) recent proposed child welfare program. When the old University Avenue armouries was there, Jack Pinkofsky used to park his car every day on the boulevard of the University Avenue Armouries. As you can expect, Mr. Speaker, anyone who parks on such a boulevard gets a parking ticket, especially when parking all day and where there is a sign which quite clearly says that you cannot park there at any time. April 26, 1988

Jack was an ingenious sort of guy, and he still is. He decided to fight the ticket, and he fought it on some very interesting grounds. He argued that the ticket was based on a municipal by-law; that the municipal by-law was passed under the authority of a provincial law; and that, in fact, the armouries property stood on federal property, not an provincial property. Therefore, municipal by-laws authorized by provincial laws did not apply to federal property.
The courts found that Jack was right and that federal property was immune from any law passed by the Province of Ontario, or authorized and passed by a municipality. Jack did not have to pay his parking ticket. He got off not because he was not parking there illegally but because of a technicality.
The Jack Pinkofsky situation is the same sort of situation which the federal Government ran into recently when a federal polluter was charged under the Province of Ontario's environmental laws with breaking those laws, being in breach of them, and thus subject to all the harsh penalties for which the Ontario environmental laws provide.
What happened in that case? We find that in the federal Department of Justice there are some ingenious people like Jack Pinkofsky and that in fact they fought and defended that case, not on the grounds that this particular federal polluter had not broken provincial law, not on the grounds that this federal polluter was not a polluter, but on the technical grounds that in fact provincial laws did not apply to federal polluters. That is the sort of defence used not only by Jack Pinkofsky with parking tickets but now by the federal Justice Department with federal polluters.
I do not know about you, Mr. Speaker, but I do not think that a federal polluter should be able to get off on technical grounds like that. It is one thing for a parking ticket, but it is an entirely different thing for something severe like that.

He said: Motion No. 4 provides a direction to the Agency that in carrying out its object-this is right after the objects clause that we just discussed-it shall ensure that there be equity between the Atlantic provinces in the allocation of resources, effort and programs in a manner to be determined by the Agency, and the Agency shall report annually to Parliament on the fulfilment of this objective.

The consequences are that these programs that were originally set up to support regional development ended up helping regional development in north Toronto, and regional development programs ended up responding to requests, demands, and lobbying from larger business enterprises.

In Newfoundland $9.4 million was spent in the whole province with a population in the range of five times more than that of Cape Breton. In Nova Scotia, exclusive of Cape Breton Island, there was an expenditure of $19 million. In Prince Edward Island $5.3 million was spent out of a total $126 million. In New Brunswick $20 million was spent.
Therefore, we have a concern that in carrying out its programs the Agency itself, which is supposed to promote the economic development of the Atlantic region, will be favouring one region or one province, or one part of a province over another. If a business enterprise, or a large number of business enterprises in the Province of Nova Scotia are ready because they have sufficient equity or have in place their business plan or market plan and have the backing and the financing for a percentage of a project and know that they can get the rest of it from ACOA, then they will be off and running. Mr. Speaker, the honey industry is divided on the issue of the ban on importation of honey bees from the United States and has been for some time. Its national body, the Canadian Honey Council, has not taken a consensus position to provide advice to the Government. Instead, this issue has rested on provincial beekeepers' associations of which all but one have indicated that they are not willing to live with the risk of importing bees from the United States.
The polarization of the industry on this issue has been emphasized by the strong lobby of the beekeepers who want to import bees from the United States, and, recently, some beekeepers formed an organization called Alberta Beekeepers for Mite-Free Bees to represent the producers who favour the border closure.
Recognizing that some citizens were not well informed about the prevailing situation and to clarify facts and distribute uniform information across the country, an industry-Government meeting was held on March 23, 1988. At that time, U.S. officials in attendance outlined the progress the scientists and regulatory officers had achieved in attempting to control the varroa disease and its spread. Agriculture Canada officials are still concerned about the completeness of the scientific data and the effectiveness of regulatory measures used to assist in disease reduction in the United States. To
April 28, 1988

date, there is no indication that these will ensure 100 per cent control over the disease.
There are presently 19,000 beekeepers in Canada, of which approximately 2,000 are commercial. Together, they operate 700,000 beehives or colonies. There is a maximum of 120 commercial beekeepers who will be affected by the border closing measures, representing approximately 100,000 colonies. Of these 120 beekeepers, most are bulk honey producers and will hire about 500 people as seasonal help. At an average of 150 pounds of honey per hive, 15 million pounds of honey will be lost to production in 1988. The five-year Canadian average production is 85 million pounds. Therefore, the decrease in production is estimated at 18 per cent for an approximate value of $7 million at the current price of honey.
It is not clear how the decreased honeybee population will affect the pollination of clover and canola. While honeybees are the recommended pollinators of clovers, wild bees and leaf cutting bees also contribute to their pollination. The biology of the Canola plant also allows the plant to be productive without the presence of honeybees. This data has not been clearly researched and it would be presumptuous to attribute a dollar value to the impact of the losses of honeybees to these crops.
Alternative sources of bees have been available to supply the increased Canadian demand. Agriculture Canada officials, as well as provincial Government officials and some beekeepers, have been in close contact with New Zealand and Australia who awaited bee orders to gear up production all winter. We are familiar with the Australian animal health system and have confidence in its regulatory measures. There is no evidence that varroa and tracheal mites exist in that country and we have concluded that bees could be safely imported from both Australia and New Zealand.
Adjournment Debate
Canadian beekeepers were also willing to provide bees to their fellow package bee operators. The problem, therefore, was not one of supply, but of price. The Special Canadian Grains Program should help to ease part of the financial crisis faced by beekeepers. The Province of Alberta has offered financial assistance to all beekeepers to compensate the increased cost of honey production. Unfortunately, other prairie provinces have not accepted this responsibility, thus creating disparities between provinces.
We have concluded that a fair and equitable compensation payment cannot be made at this time. Eastern beekeepers did not receive compensation when the border east of Manitoba was closed in 1986. It must be pointed out that the Government has never compensated for actions to prevent the introduction of undesirable diseases into the country. As I have already mentioned, some relief will be forthcoming from the Special Canadian Grains Program and should help to alleviate the financial burden facing many honey producers. A meeting on tripartite stabilization was held at the beginning of the month. If provinces and beekeepers agree on the program, there is a strong possibility it could be in place for the 1988 marketing season.
As you can see, Mr. Speaker, positive actions have been triggered by the setbacks the industry faces and I assure you that the Government will continue to work with the industry to build a strong sector.

It amends the Constitution Act in order to do certain things without saying how it should be amended. It only says that it is to be amended in order to give some protection to the right to enjoy property and that the federal Government and the provinces will work it out in some fashion. That is all it says.
The original motion by the Hon. Member for Kitchener was very explicit on how this House should amend the Constitution Act, 1982, namely, by adding within Section 7 of the Charter the words "enjoyment of property". I find it very strange that the Conservative Party should now be welshing on that very specific proposal.
I can only conclude that the Conservative Party has been listening to the arguments put forward by the New Democratic Party during the course of the previous four hours of debate on this matter and has concluded that the motion originally proposed by the Hon. Member for Kitchener-and the

April 29, 1988
Property Rights
amendment that was proposed in earlier Parliaments, is very inadvisable; that it could indeed lead to very perverse results and might circumscribe the rights of all citizens, including other property owners. It might also make difficult the enjoyment of all freedoms guaranteed in the Charter. The matter needs a good deal more discussion and debate and, ideally, the matter needs to be dropped.
Those who advocate amending the Charter of Rights and Freedoms to guarantee the right to enjoy property are, in my view, being either mischievious or naive. When they make this proposal they make it sound as though it was the most simple of adjustments, a statement of the obvious that would be opposed only by someone who wants to deprive people of what is rightfully theirs. That is the subtle implication. Yet, as many associations have pointed out including the Canadian Civil Liberties Association, entrenching property rights or the rights to the enjoyment of property can have very perverse results.
The Hon. Member for Ottawa-Carleton is under the impression that property means land and land only. That is ridiculous. Property in this modern day and age means a great deal more than land, the most important of which is intellectual property. That in itself indicates that property rights are a far less clear-cut concept than other rights already entrenched in the Constitution.
For example, when we speak of the right not to be imprisoned without due process of law or the right to freedom of expression, we know at least in a general sense what is intended. But, what actually is the right to enjoy property? That right needs to be so hedged with restrictions in order to protect the rights of others, and of society as a whole that it is far, far from absolute.
What then would it mean to enshrine in our Constitution as a fundamental and more or less absolute right the enjoyment of property? If it meant only that the right to enjoy property existed to the extent that society through its laws chooses not to limit it-and that in effect is the situation today-then the constitutional guarantee would be virtually meaningless. If it meant more than that, then the still insufficiently explored consequence could be a dismantling of some or even all of the laws that exist to protect us all.
That is why we have suspected for some time that what the promoters of the property amendment really want is a legal opportunity to challenge a vast body of legislation which exists today and which subjects property ownership to a wider community interest, including that of other property owners.
Urban property speculators, for instance, are thirsting to use a property rights clause to short circuit zoning by-laws and community organizations, those organizations having the gall to prevent landowners from doing whatever they please with their property. They do not want to see the freedom-putting freedom in quotes-to build a fast food stand in a quiet neighbourhood abridged. They do not want to have any
limitations on their intention, perhaps, to turn the back 40 into a highly profitable dump for PCBs. If property rights are constitutionally entrenched, how long would it take for a lawyer to draft a brief denouncing rent controls as unconscionable and illegal government meddling?
In its current form the enjoyment of property-and what was a proposed amendment and which now has been somehow taken off the table by the Conservatives-could easily be used to throw into question zoning by-laws, restrictions on land use, rent controls, environmental laws, restrictions on foreign ownership, the right of Governments to expropriate property in the public interest, and who knows what else. It is understandable why most provincial Governments, many of them Conservative-and it is the provinces which have a large voice in property and civil rights under Section 92 of the Constitution-have hitherto said, including the former Premier of Alberta, that the placing of the enjoyment of property in the Constitution should be avoided and must be opposed. That is of course what this Party intends to do.

Speech:
Mr. Speaker, I listened with interest to my hon. friend and to the Hon. Member for Athabasca (Mr. Shields) before him. I notice that we have debated the Bill on western diversification for about five hours. I am curious that members of the Government would consider a five hour debate to be excessive, too much, a filibuster, wrong-headed and inappropriate. I wonder if Canadians who are watching us on their television sets and from the gallery would consider five hours of debate on a major western economic initiative to be an excessive amount of debate.
I want to remind my hon. friend opposite that a democracy is not the most efficient system of government. The most efficient system of government is that which is found in totalitarian regimes and military dictatorships where they do not have to bother with Parliament and where members of the Government do not have to bother with members of the Opposition. Government members can ignore the people of Canada and their concerns. That is the most efficient system of government, but we do not have that system in Canada.
The Conservatives are attempting in devious ways to turn this into a totalitarian form of government where there is no debate in the House of Commons. My hon. friend was not here at that time, so I certainly do not hold him responsible for the behaviour of his colleagues before him, but I remember the day in this House when the Members of Parliament, duly elected by the people of Canada, were presented with the spectacle of a whole group of Conservative Members of Parliament rushing the Speaker's chair, brandishing their fists in his face and saying that they would bring Parliament to its knees.
I remember that day. I must say that it was one of the saddest days of my life. I was saddened to think that people who were elected to represent their views had decided that it

May 3, 1988
Western Economic Diversification Act
was appropriate to stop Parliament from functioning. Day after day after day, the bells rang. Parliament was muzzled. The heavy jackboots of the Conservative Party had been brought down on the necks of parliamentarians. There was no opportunity to debate, there was no opportunity to ask questions.
I know that this is a touchy issue for some Conservative Members, and I recognize that most Members here were not there at that time, but that is the kind of Government we are now beginning to see take form. After five hours of debate on third reading of the Western Diversification Bill, Members are saying that this is excessive, that Members of Parliament should not debate this for more than a few minutes.
There are 282 Members of Parliament here. Not all Members of Parliament will speak on a piece of legislation, but there are four or five Members from the New Democratic Party, four or five Members from the Liberal Party and four or five Members from the Conservative Party who want to express their views. However, the Government is saying that it will muzzle those Members. It does not want to hear the views of those who represent the people of Canada.
I just want to say that every time the Government attempts to muzzle Parliament, to choke off the voice of the people, we are going to remind people of what is going on. That is what is going on now. The Government is trying to bring to a premature end the thoughtful, positive debate on the Western Diversification Fund. I want to say very clearly that we support the Bill. We are going to vote in favour of it. We will probably vote unanimously in favour of the initiative because we think at least the principle is a good one. However, we have many concerns which have been raised by my hon. colleagues such as whether the best way to spend taxpayers' money through this fund is by giving $9.5 million to one of the largest pulp and paper consortiums in the world. Would it not go ahead without that money? Other smaller businesses are being denied funds. Those are the questions we want to pose at the close of this debate.
Again, I want to remind the people of Canada that we have seen some dictatorial tactics and antics by the Conservative Party in the past and we are seeing them again. They have a complete disregard for what democracy is. They have a complete disregard for the traditions of Parliament. We will always oppose dictatorial practices by the Conservative Government whenever and wherever they take place.

Frankly, I believe this Bill would be much better if some of those amendments had been accepted.
Criminal Code
There are three important aspects to dealing with crime in a community like Essex-Windsor. First, citizens and citizens' groups should be drawn into the process of assisting police and the community at large in dealing with crime. We have had a very active Crime Stoppers program, which has involved careful surveillance of different neighbourhoods that are subject to higher levels of crime than other parts of our community. There is also a system by which those who have information about a particular crime could make confidential reports to the police to help solve these particular crimes. That kind of public approach is an important step forward in dealing with a very serious problem in my community and others.
Other citizens in our community who are concerned about the problems of victims of crime have organized groups to deal with child abuse. Last year, an important conference was held in Essex-Windsor in which the various difficulties which afflict victims of child abuse were outlined, not just in the immediate instance of the abuse being suffered but in terms of the psychological damage that goes on far into the future.
Such child abuse is at the very heart of an attempt to respond to victims of crime in our society.
Finally, I want to speak about problems of public awareness and the difficulties that are brought to bear on victims of crime in our community.
