Mr. Speaker, although I respect the right of the Hon. Member for Broadview-Greenwood (Ms. McDonald) to interpret the free trade agreement as she sees fit, 1 simply cannot-and I say this at as a politician historian-concur with her assessment that the political sovereignty of Canada is in any way in jeopardy as a result of the agreement. However, the specific question before the House today relates to the cultural community and industry in general, and that is the point I would like to address.
We on the government side believe that our cultural industries are exempt from the free trade agreement, including Canada's publishing, film and video, music and sound recording, broadcasting and cable industries. The Government, as promised, has maintained all existing cultural support measures for cultural industries, as well as the ability to introduce new ones.
There are four specific undertakings in the free trade agreement touched upon by the Hon. Member. She identified them. We do not believe the ones identified by the Hon. Member have anything to do with the cultural role of these industries, and there are no other undertakings in the agreement which will apply to the cultural industries.

May 9, 1988
Adjournment Debate
The exemption for the cultural industries makes it clear that the free trade agreement will not in any way limit our flexibility to introduce special measures to assist these industries, as required now or in the future.
Last week the Minister of Communications (Miss MacDonald) announced policies which were referred to by the Hon. Member in rather disparaging terms, with respect to new investment policies for the film industry and $200 million in new support programs to assist the production, promotion, and marketing of Canadian film and videos. The Minister also announced that she will shortly table legislation, as promised, to ensure that Canada operates a separate national distribution market. Through the additional funding and legislation to regulate the importation of films and videos, the Government has reaffirmed its commitment to the industry.
This policy was not negotiated as part of the free trade agreement. It is a Canadian solution to Canadian problems, developed in consultation with the film industry in Canada and around the world. Despite attempts by the Americans to raise the issue, Canada's cultural industries, including the film distribution issue, were kept off the bargaining table.
The free trade agreement will not in any way affect our ability to continue to develop cultural policies for Canada. In particular, the claim that the agreement will encourage U.S. retaliation against our future cultural policies is groundless. In fact, the opposite is true. At the moment the United States is free to take unilateral action against Canada in retaliation for what it considers to be unfair trade practices. The agreement will improve the situation, by placing some constraints on the ability of Congress to take action against any of our so-called cultural trade barriers. The United States will be required to demonstrate that a Canadian measure in fact contravenes the trade agreement. United States retaliation must be limited to a measure of equivalent commercial effect.
Furthermore, the U.S. will not be able to act unilaterally, as it can now. Advance notification and consultations with Canada would have to take place, in accordance with provisions in the agreement. The trade agreement is about trade, it is not about culture. It is a commercial arrangement that will put our economic relationship with the United States on a secure footing. Our culture can only gain from the stronger Canada that will result from this agreement.

Mr. Speaker, 1 am pleased to take part in this debate on the motion of my colleague, the Hon. Member for Medicine Hat (Mr. Porter). The motion before the House calls upon the Government to give special consideration to the 1984 report of the Special Joint Committee on Senate Reform.
This is a most timely debate, especially for those of us from Alberta. It is now just over a year since the signing of the Meech Lake Accord on April 30, 1987. The Accord represents the beginning of a new era in Canadian federalism. As well as bringing Quebec into the constitutional family, the Accord provides new constitutional and institutional arrangements to
Senate Reform
encourage closer, more harmonious relations between the federal and provincial governments.
One of the most significant aspects of the Accord is its commitment to further constitutional reform and to Senate reform in particular. It is to this issue specifically that I address my comments this afternoon.
As Hon. Members will be aware, the constitutional Accord of June 3, 1987, provides for an entrenched second round of discussions aimed at fostering further constitutional development. In particular, the Accord requires the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) to convene a First Ministers' Conference on the Constitution at least once a year once the Meech Lake amendments have been proclaimed. Among the items on the agenda for these conferences will be Senate reform. This will include the role and functions of the Senate; the powers of the Senate; the method of selecting Senators; representation in the Senate.
As a result of a change in the amending formula, the consent of all provinces will be required for amendments to these matters. In future, each province will have an equal say on this vital issue. This contrasts with the present arrangement which grants a veto to Ontario and Quebec acting together, but not to any other two provinces acting together.
Finally, as a demonstration of the Prime Minister's good faith and commitment, the Accord provides that until constitutional amendments on the Senate are achieved, the federal Government will appoint Senators from among candidates proposed by provincial Governments and who are acceptable to the federal Government. The provinces thus will have a real say on appointments to the Senate until more comprehensive reform is achieved.
Contrary to what some critics of the Accord have suggested, the Accord provides for the full and open discussion that I believe all aspects of Senate reform deserve. It assures that all the major points that need to be addressed must be considered at annual First Ministers' Conferences.
Senate reform has been the subject of many studies and reports over the years. The report of the Special Joint Committee on Senate Reform was an important and useful contribution to this ongoing question. It recommended that the Senate be directly elected in order to "strengthen the authority of Parliament to speak and act on behalf of Canadians in all parts of the country".
The Hon. Member for Lethbridge-Foothills (Mr. Thacker) was a distinguished member of the Special Joint Committee which tabled its report in January, 1984. The report called for a directly elected Senate, with a weighted representation of seats to increase regional representation. Senators would be elected for a single nine-year term, with one-third of the Senators elected every three years. The Senate would have a 120-day suspensive veto over ordinary legislation, and ratification authority over Order in Council appointments to federal agencies with important regional implications.

Government Organization Act, Atlantic Canada, 1987

Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to comment briefly on Bill C-105. Again, there was full co-operation on both sides when this Bill was considered in committee. The measures proposed in this Bill are long overdue, and it is too bad the accident at Hinton happened before we started this exercise. Mr. Speaker, I welcome the inclusion in this Bill of many of the recommendations of the Foisy Report, such as providing for rest periods, which is already being done. The report's recommendation for a new safety mechanism instead of the dead man's brake has also been implemented. The new system requires some kind of activity in the locomotive compartment, and otherwise the train stops automatically. So this measure has already been put into effect.
Judge Foisy also recommended including a provision that already exists under the Aeronautics Act, namely that physicians disclose any potentially hazardous condition an employee may have. The Bill acts on this recommendation as well. This is a very important measure, Mr. Speaker. The legislation would apply to designated categories of employees. When the employees consult their family doctor, if according to the latter, the patient has a condition that would be a threat to safe operations, he will have to point this out to the medical authorities of the railway company.
We did have some reservations and we wanted to be sure that in this case, the employee would be the first to be notified.
During our discussions in committee, committee members agreed to amend the Bill to ensure that reasonable steps were taken to first inform the person concerned, the employee.
This Bill also tells us that inspection, compliance, and enforcement of railway safety standards will be improved by granting broader powers to inspectors. What the Government does not tell us is that the present number of inspectors is probably not quite adequate. To ensure that safety is taken seriously, the Government will have to provide the necessary funding to employ inspectors in sufficient numbers so that they can carry out their responsibilities. This is definitely a priority, Mr. Speaker.
The report published on the use of drugs by railway employees is a clear indication that we must proceed with certain measures, and everyone seems to agree, employers, unions and workers. I consider it essential that assistance programs be set up for employees who are addicted to drugs or alcohol. That is why, Mr. Speaker, I proposed an amendment to Section 18 of the Bill, which was intended to establish and finance such programs. After discussion in committee, the proposal was reformulated and accepted. I believe that this amendment, Mr. Speaker, was most positive.
The environment is also a subject of concern to everyone; it is of great concern to the members of my party, Mr. Speaker. This Bill may also have an impact on the environment and that
May 17, 1988

is why I have suggested some amendments. For example, paragraph 24(l)(e) of the Bill concerns the removal of trees, brush and weeds on railway lines. I have suggested that alternatives to chemicals be used for this purpose.
I consider this matter to be very important, Mr. Speaker, and I thank the members of the Committee for having kindly accepted this recommendation.
1 also propose that Clause 41 of the Bill be amended in order that heavier fines would be levied in cases of contravention. This was also approved by the members of the committee.
Another matter the committee agreed upon was to ensure that there would be good representation of all concerned groups on the new railway safety consultative committee. This was also agreed to by all members of the committee.
The committee also agreed to retain Section 1 of the Railway Relocation and Crossing Act. Mr. Speaker, I asked the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp) some days back about the guidelines on research involving human subjects, because just at that time the Medical Research Council of Canada had adopted a report dealing with that subject. This document is extremely timely because it raises central issues respecting the protection of human life in society.
The Medical Research Council accepted the report which I hold here as the MRC's guidelines on research involving human subjects. It requires all research funds to be in compliance with these guidelines.
By way of introduction, let me briefly make a few comments about this report and the guidelines. First, it is very clear that this document, and the members of the Medical Research Council Standing Committee on Ethics in Experimentation who authored it are experts in the subject. They come from diverse backgrounds reflecting medical, legal, ethical, theolog-ic, and scientific backgrounds. No one can take lightly the conclusions they come to in the report. I would defer personally to any of them on this subject. I do not raise this subject in

May 17, 1988
Adjournment Debate
Parliament as an expert but simply as a concerned Canadian who sees many straws in the wind and an historic opportunity to weave those straws together into something new, a human life Act.
This document further sets out a fundamental principle on page 12:
The Standing Committee believes that the basic ethical principle in research, as in health care, is respect for life. From this principle flow others: the concept of autonomy, the duty to beneficence, and the duty to justice.
From the principles one quickly gets into the practicalities. We find, for example, on page 32, with regard to research with fetuses and embryos, the following:
At this time, the legal status of embryos and fetuses is not well-defined, nor is the social consensus. While issues of consent and autonomy may not therefore apply, clear ethical concerns arise from the inarguable fact that embryos and fetuses are human life forms.
Finally, I would refer to page 11 of this document which gave rise to my question to the Minister wherein the standing committee states its belief as follows:
... at this time the use of Guidelines within the current body of law is sufficient to reinforce the ethical conduct of research with human subjects.
The significant phrase there is "within the current body of law". It is at this juncture that I submit the Medical Research Council of Canada and those adopting this approach of guidelines only in this difficult area of human experimentation are perhaps pushing an empty wheelbarrow. To say that guidelines will suffice within the body of existing law is to refer to something that truly does not exist. The existing body of law in this area is clearly unsettled.
That is why I advocated on February 4 in this Flouse the formation of a new federal statute which 1 call the human life Act. It would draw together in a single statute all aspects of intentional intervention in the human life cycle.
It would deal not only with the question of abortion, which is so galvanizing this country and this Parliament these days, but with other questions such as genetic engineering, surrogate motherhood, euthanasia, and on and on the list goes. The newspapers are full of it. The Toronto Star of March 29, 1988 had an article headlined "Genetic Tests Open Scary World of Super-Species". The subheading is "Gene-Splicing Promises Society Huge Pay-Offs, But Others Fear Biological Chaos".
We even have the religious press replete with concerns expressed on this subject. For example, the April issue of The United Church Observer had a series of articles under the general heading "Manufacturing a Miracle". One week after I called for a human life Act, the West German Government announced plans to ban research on human embryos, outlaw surrogacy, and curb artificial insemination. The new legislation will forbid surrogate motherhood, production of human embryos for research, measures allowing the choice of a child's sex in artificial insemination, and attempts to breed mixtures of humans and animals.
We have the Canadian Coalition for Reproductive Technologies seeking a royal commission on this subject. It states in its documents that as a society we are not ready to pass laws and that we need first to do the necessary research and engage in a broad, informed national debate. That debate is under way, and I want to see it brought to the floor of the House of Commons in new legislation that can encompass all these questions. The debate will take place this summer at the Fifty-Seventh Couchiching Conference, a well-known national forum for dialogue on public issues. That conference will deal with biological engineering, a blessing or curse.
I have been in touch with David Suzuki who popularizes questions of scientific research in this country. He has gone back to the whole question of genetic engineering and what the Nazis were busy with under the guise of science in Germany in the 1930s. That had as its dimension on one hand the elimination of millions of people, and on the other hand the biological efforts to create a master race. In a letter to me dated May 10, David Suzuki says:
I think you've raised a very important issue and I agree we must not get
bogged down on abortion alone. We have acquired great manipulative powers
that take us into completely uncharted territory. I believe we need a Royal
Commission to look at the issue.
Please press on with your efforts.
Be it a royal commission, be it Bill C-107 dealing with patenting forms of human life, be it the report of the Law Reform Commission, I have much more on this subject that 1 want to bring forward in the discussion. However, given my limited time, I call upon the Government to take a broader initiative at this time and set all this discussion in the framework of a new human life Act.

Mr. Speaker, the federal Government is committed to finding a real and lasting solution to the serious environmental and economic damage being caused by acid rain. That is why our Government, unlike the previous Government, has implemented major emission reductions in Canada and has pressed the United States for targeted, mandated emission reductions necessary to stop damage to the Canadian environment.

Speech:
Mr. Speaker, I have the honour of moving second reading of Bill C-126. The purpose of this Bill is to amend the Bretton Woods and Related Agreements Act. The proposed Act will provide the parliamentary authority for Canada's contribution to the International Monetary Fund's Enhanced Structural Adjustment Facility. It will authorize the Minister of Finance to lend and grant funds to the enhanced structural facility trust on behalf of the Government of Canada. I am very pleased that this morning I will be able to explain this Bill to Members of the House.

The creation of this facility is an important measure taken by the IMF to deal with the debt problems of the world's least developed countries. This mechanism will add significantly to the structural adjustment facility set up in 1986 to help low-income countries balance their payments on very favorable terms.
After the enhanced structural adjustment facility was implemented, the size of the balance of payments problems of the least developed countries led to requests for additional help. It became obvious that international organizations would have to take further special measures to deal with the problems of the poorest debtor countries, especially those of the Sahel. Their extremely slow economic development and the weak growth of their export markets seriously undermined their recovery efforts. Their debt burden had become a major obstacle to their economic development.
Faced with this bleak economic outlook, some developing countries hesitated to pursue or begin sustained adjustment initiatives under the International Monetary Fund. It became obvious that these countries would need increased financial aid on favorable terms to effectively implement through reforms. Although the resources of the structural adjustment facility were limited, they were an appropriate form of assistance because the more favorable terms and extended repayment schedules offered by the structural adjustment facility, as compared to a simple loan, are necessary to help these fragile economies adjust. Increasing the resources of the structural adjustment facility was therefore suggested.

The initiative for an Enhanced Structural Adjustment Facility received the endorsement of the group of seven

May 20, 1988
Bretton Woods and Related Agreements Act
industrialized countries at the Venice Summit in June, 1987. At that time, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) expressed Canada's support for such a facility. The result of the international consensus to provide more aid to the poorest debtor countries has been a tripling of the IMF structural adjustment facility. This facility is being enhanced and increased to an important degree.
The Enhanced Structural Adjustment Facility is expected to add over $10 billion in equivalent Canadian funds to the resources available through the IMF structural adjustment facility. The loans will carry a subsidized interest rate of one-half per cent per annum and will be repaid over 10 years. The loans are conditional upon countries having an IMF-supported structural reform program in place. The programs will be formulated within a policy framework worked out jointly by the borrowing country, the IMF, and the World Bank. Potentially some 60 very poor countries could benefit from the use of the Enhanced Structural Adjustment Facility resources.
The Enhanced Structural Adjustment Facility contributions are made to two accounts. The contributions to the loan account will earn interest. Contributions to the subsidy account will be in the form of grants and allow the IMF to lend loan account funds at one-half per cent interest per year. The Enhanced Structural Adjustment Facility has received the enthusiastic support of the international community. Some 25 countries have made pledges to this facility.
In Canada's case, the Bill before us will give the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson), the authority to lend up to $550 million Canadian to the loan account. These moneys will be lent in three equal instalments over three years beginning in 1988. This contribution will pay Canada a rate of interest based on long-term rates for domestic financial instruments of five major world currencies.
The legislation will further allow for the Minister of Finance to grant up to $250 million Canadian over the 12-year life of the trust, in order that our loan contribution can be loaned out to low-income countries at one-half per cent interest per year. Canada's contribution will be financed through the Consolidated Revenue Fund. The subsidy portion will be counted as part of Canada's official development assistance. The legislation allows changes to both the subsidy and loan contributions, through Order-in-Council, to reflect future international discussions.
As a Government we support the structural adjustment facility because we believe that countries that are undertaking necessary adjustments in their economic policies deserve the encouragement of the international community. This is particularly true when required policy reforms may be politically unpopular in the short term. Furthermore, the Enhanced Structural Adjustment Facility will be complementary to our bilateral aid efforts. The economic stabilization of the least developed economies, quite frankly, is a necessary prerequisite to their more effective use of bilateral aid.
For all those reasons, this Bill deserves our strong support.

Perhaps if the Hon. Member would let me finish explaining the process the NDP goes through. In advance of conventions, riding associations as well as some of the affiliated organizations will pass resolutions and send them to convention. At convention, every delegate will get a book of resolutions that have been proposed by the rank and file of the Party for consideration by convention.
We have a resolutions committee that will sift through the proposed resolutions, look at previous resolutions that had been adopted to determine if they are still relevant, and try to weed out any conflicts. We admit that from time to time there have been conflicts, in terms of the wording, which have only been discovered later on.
That committee reports to convention and indicates an order of priority of the resolutions for debate. That is debated as well, because sometimes people would like their particular issue moved up on the agenda.
Ultimately, some resolutions are debated at convention. We never have enough time to debate every resolution in the resolutions book. Hundreds of resolutions are submitted to our federal and provincial conventions.
The other point is that those resolutions which are not dealt with at convention are automatically referred to our federal council for consideration. For example, at our last convention in Montreal in 1987, a resolution that I had drafted and submitted from my riding association had not been dealt with by the floor. It was later referred to the federal council which, in turn, adopted it in a different form. I simply want people to understand the process.
We have provincial conventions that make decisions which are not necessarily binding on the federal Party or caucus until those policies have been adopted by the convention. Resolution No. 5 adopted by the federal council of NDP in 1983, reads:
The immediate protection of jobs in the industry through import restrictions
to ensure Canadian industry at least its present share of the domestic market
until the removal of such restrictions is warranted by:
(a)	improved productivity and competitiveness of the Canadian economy as a whole; and
(b)	proven adherence of competitor nations to recognized standards of human rights and economic justice as adopted by the I.L.O. in the form of Convention and Recommendations.
That is the operative resolution by which we are governed.
I support my colleague, the Hon. Member for Spadina (Mr. Heap), in his ongoing attempt to assist workers in the apparel industry. I know his interest in their ability to keep their jobs, as well as obtain decent pay, and to have some protection from the kind of competition we are seeing from other countries which are paying in a day what we do not consider legal pay for an hour's work.
The Hon. Member for Spadina has proposed in Bill C-243 that as a manufacturer expands his operation and requires additional materials from offshore he be allowed to do so in
proportion to the amount of sales and manufacturing. I think that makes a lot of sense.
The Liberal spokesperson suggested that there may be some things wrong with the Bill but the general concept of it was worth pursuing. He hoped that there would be a mechanism to allow the substance of this Bill to be sent to a committee for further consideration.
I believe the Parliamentary Secretary also indicated the importance of this industry and of trying to enhance it. We may disagree on the direction we should take, but perhaps there is a willingness to consider transferring the subject matter to a standing committee. Perhaps members on the Government side will want to consider that option.
In conclusion, I support Bill C-243. I wanted to clarify the process of how the NDP develops its resolutions, and I wanted to caution Members not to mix resolutions proposed with resolutions passed.

I know only too well of some of those by-laws that the former Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development passed that became tied up in the courts in relation to the Gitksan-Wet'suwet'en by-laws on the Skeena.

The Joint Committee's general findings as to the degree of conformity of many by-laws to its scrutiny criteria are recorded in the correspondence reproduced in Appendix 'B' to this report. Air Canada has been a money maker, but of course if there is one thing that the Tory back-benchers and many of the Tory Cabinet hate worse than a Crown corporation that loses money, it is a Crown corporation that makes money. A recent poll indicated that 53 per cent of the Canadian people oppose the sale of Air Canada. It had a very good image. This poll done by Angus-Reid showed that federal Progressive Conservative supporters are almost evenly divided on the Air Canada issue. Forty-seven per cent oppose selling it and 44 per cent are in favour. Even those people who traditionally vote Conservative, but are not necessarily as hide-bound as are some of the Conservative Members, on balance recognize that selling Air Canada does not make a lot of sense.
This is only a partial sale. Forty-five per cent is being sold with 55 per cent being left with the Government. The Government's shares will vote with the majority. In other words, the 55 per cent share which the Government is retaining in our name will not be voted in accordance with our interests. What we have here is neither fish, fowl, nor good red herring. It is a lame duck corporation and will be flying with one wing. It will be 45 per cent private and 55 per cent public, but the 55 per cent public will be non-voting shares.
We have to ask how that can possibly serve the public interest. If the 45 per cent wish to shut down unprofitable routes, the 55 per cent of government shares will simply go along with it. The public is, in effect, left holding a 55 per cent bag and has no say in it.
A year ago the Minister for International Trade (Mr. Crosbie), who is sometimes able to speak the truth when other members of the Government are not, said that it would be better to sell all of it or none of it. Of course, we are selling a little bit of it. We are selling 45 per cent of it.
The Government pretends to have it both ways. It says it wants to protect the public interest. It says that it is protecting the interests of places like Winnipeg, that servicing will continue to take place there. It says that it will protect employee benefits and pensions. On the other hand, it says that it is getting out of the business and the business will be open to private direction. This is privatization on a wing and a prayer.
What possible reasons are there for privatizing? One of them, of course, is the need for equity. Everyone recognizes
that Air Canada needs new equipment and needs equity. Certainly privatizing is not the only way in which that could be done. Another possible reason is to reduce the deficit. This will not result in a significant reduction in the deficit. We are getting rid of a corporation which has in fact brought money into the Treasury.
In conclusion, it is important that all Members of this House recognize the importance of Air Canada as a Crown corporation over the last 50 years. It served the public purpose. It has been one of the building blocks of Canadian Confederation. Canada is a huge country, it stretches thousands of miles from the Atlantic to the Pacific and needs something like Air Canada to tie it together. It has served that purpose in the past and we need to have that purpose served in the future. This is not an easy country to hold together. We are talking about a new constitution for Canada. I submit that infrastructure such as Air Canada is as important in holding Canada together as is the Constitution. Yet the Government is getting rid of it.
Air Canada has set service, safety, and employment standards for the airline industry. It is responsible, not only for a financial bottom line but to serve social purpose. On that basis I do not think the Conservative arguments for selling Air Canada are reasonable, I do not think they are convincing. On the contrary, I think there are very convincing reasons for keeping Air Canada as a Crown corporation. We will continue to oppose this sell-off and sell-out.

Mr. Speaker, today I would like to give my assessment of the problem of organized crime. First of all, I would like to say that the Hon. Member for Trinity (Miss Nicholson) is right to be concerned about organized crime in Canada. My only criticism is the solution she suggests. In fact, an inquiry of this type would be more appropriate in the United States, where fragmented attempts to enforce legislation, lack of co-ordination, states' rights and many other elements make it very difficult to discover the extent of the problem posed by organized crime.
In Canada, we are lucky to have a very co-operative system under which policing, prosecution and enforcement bodies exchange information and co-operate in their operations. Thanks to this network we have a very clear understanding of the problem we are dealing with.
The many information sources at our disposal include the annual report prepared by Criminal Intelligence Service Canada, published by the committee on organized crime of the Canadian Association of Chiefs of Police; the annual RCMP report on drugs, Customs Canada's drugs seizure report; and the excellent reports prepared by the various services in Quebec and British Columbia dealing with organized crime. According to these sources, organized crime is not beaten but at least there is little chance it will expand.
In recent years, motorcycle gangs have been a major problem. They have become involved in all forms of organized crime, including drug trafficking, prostitution and contract killings.
The major gangs are very business-like. They increase their numbers by taking over smaller ones. Many bikers have shed the image of the sloppily-dressed trouble-maker and become clever, extremely image-conscious businessmen. The big crime organizations are also present in Canada. The most important members work in central and western Canada, but they often have contacts in many other countries. These groups are involved in what are often referred to as consensual crimes, in other words, customers agree to purchase the illicit goods or services they are offered. These crimes include drug trafficking, prostitution, gambling and loan sharking.
Although the Atlantic provinces appear to be relatively untouched by the more insidious forms of organized crime, there is nevertheless a thriving business in cigarette and alcohol smuggling. The region is also used as a dropping-off point for large cargoes of soft drugs, most of which come from the Caribbean. Youth gangs are also involved in organized

June 3, 1988
Organized Crime
crime activities and concentrate on gambling, drug trafficking and extortion. Occasionally, intense rivalry among gangs lead to multiple killings.
In a way, these gangs are similar to the motorcycle gangs. Since 1920, sociologists have held the view that youth gangs are often the first step towards much greater involvement in organized crime.
It is essential that measures be taken to prevent new generations of criminals, but I don't think an inquiry on organized crime is the answer. The emphasis must be on education and jobs.
By reducing the unemployment rate and by stressing the needs of Canada's youth, this Government has done a great deal to create a socio-economic climate that is not favourable for the development of organized crime.
Organized crime is a problem in most countries throughout the world. Even East Block countries will admit it exists there as well. There is an international network that focusses on dealing with these problems on a worldwide basis.
Thanks to this mechanism we are familiar with the problems of other countries, and it is reassuring to find that, compared to most countries, Canada has not been overrun by organized crime. Our parliamentary system, and our custom of appointing judges, Crown counsels, police officers and administrators according to merit, have given us a tradition of loyal public servants. It is one of our best defences against organized crime. We have a judicial system that we can trust and of which we can be proud. However, we must be prepared to provide the material assistance that goes along with that trust and that pride. We cannot ask our police officers, our Crown counsels and our judges to keep fighting organized crime without giving them the necessary tools, and today, these include the authority to participate with other countries in a form of judicial cooperation, and also the authority to declare forfeit the financial proceeds of organized crime. The House can give them those tools by adopting Bills C-68 and C-61. We should focus our efforts on supporting our judicial system, instead of ignoring its needs and creating a parliamentary task force.

questions to the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp) of May 18 regarding the need for government leadership and funding in the urgent fight against the AIDS epidemic. Nearly 1,000 Canadians have died of AIDS. Nearly 800 others are diagnosed as having AIDS and an estimated further
50,000	people are carrying the HIV virus. Only now is the federal Government starting to fund a comprehensive attack on this dreadful epidemic.

While it is a welcome beginning, the Government must realize that it is only a first step toward a full-scale fight against AIDS. Second, we are worried that the funds may not be directed appropriately and efficiently in the all out campaign against AIDS that is required. All the money in the world will not turn the tide against AIDS if it is squandered, if government policies are misdirected, or if the Government lacks the political will to address sensitive issues such as contraception in very direct, explicit ways.
Third, I am convinced by my consultations with the medical health officer in Vancouver that the most appropriate and effective way of co-ordinating both public education and support programs for AIDS patients is through the metropolitan and regional health centres, which should co-ordinate their efforts nationally and share successful techniques. They are doing the job now, they have lots of ideas, but they have not had the funds to get going in a comprehensive way.
Therefore, I urge the Minister to decentralize funding through local health authorities in major centres where there is a concentration of AIDS. -double-blind trials are largely used to compare a new drug with a similar drug which is in use. The new drug may be more effective or have fewer side-effects but the problem is to check if there is an improvement over the proven drug.

Madam Speaker, I wish first of all tonight to congratulate the Hon. Member for Laval-des-Rapides (Mr. Garneau) after listening very carefully to his comments. I wish as well to address a few points he made during his speech.
He mentioned the idea of a referendum, rejecting it on the grounds that a majority would impress its will upon a minority. Such is the danger, as he described it, of calling for the opinion of the people in a union of governments and citizens.
It may be that my knowledge of the referendum concept suffers some want. But I still believe in the possibility that during a referendum process minorities might be protected in some way. For instance, a majority of votes could be the rule in each and every area throughout the country. The danger he mentioned might then be stunted. However, in order to settle a disagreement, he admits there still exists a possibility, in a union of governments, to finally let the people decide upon the issue.
Secondly, he talked about the unanimity clause as having been recognized by the Supreme Court. Madam Speaker, to my opinion which stands to be corrected, the Supreme Court found that there was no such unanimity clause. The Member went on to say that at the time, federal Government kept to a strict interpretation of the decision.
On the contrary, in 1981 the Canadian Government decided to meet again with the provinces because the Supreme Court had resolved that unanimity was unnecessary and that the Federal could go ahead with the support of only some of the provinces.
No one knew for sure the exact number of provinces required, and maybe the federal Government could have proceeded with only two of them, namely perhaps Ontario and New Brunswick. Nevertheless, the Canadian Government decided then to try again with all the provinces and see if unanimity or, at least, a large consensus could not be achieved.
Those are the two points I wanted to address by giving my own assessment of the facts.

Madam Speaker, I wish to draw your attention to a specific Standing Order, 10(2), because that is really the one that has to be interpreted. It reads:
(2) Not more than two hours after the commencement of proceedings thereon, the Speaker shall put every question necessary to dispose of the said motion.
I think that we should take "after the commencement of proceedings" to mean two hours of actual debate. That is what it means. It means that the debate cannot take more than two hours. It does not mean that the debate cannot be interrupted by a lunch break or the normal adjournment of the House, like this evening, and be continued the next morning. What it means is that when Members have debated this question for a period of not more than two hours, the Chair has no choice.
The Speaker who is in the Chair must then rise, interrupt the proceedings and put every question necessary to dispose of the motion. I therefore maintain that since it is now after six o'clock-to continue along the same lines as my colleague from Ottawa-Vanier-the normal time for adjournment, the Chair should adjourn the House and continue tomorrow, in the first hour of the sitting, the debate on the motion very properly moved by the Hon. Member for Kamloops-Shuswap. In this way, Members will have their right to debate the motion for a full two hours, the Chair will comply with the Standing Order by putting every question necessary to dispose of the motion

before the House and the Chair will also comply with another Standing Order, namely that at six o'clock on a day like today, we call it quits.

This is where the problem has been, when a number of people have claimed refugee status, some of them being bogus claimants, and we did not have an adequate system for dealing with that. Thus we have built up a backlog of people who are claimants for refugee status, some legitimate and a great many of whom we all admit are not legitimate.
What the Government has done over the last number of years, beginning with the Liberal Government, has been inadequate to deal with this situation. The Liberal Government appointed a royal commission under Rabbi Plaut to investigate this matter. He brought in a very good report in 1985. They would have resulted in a much shorter, more expeditious process, but it would still have been a fair process for refugee claimants, a process which would have given them full access to a hearing within Canada. They would also have a fair appeal process.

Finally, I want to respond to a point which has been made by the Opposition over and over again, that is, that Order No. 26 represents tyranny by the majority. It is a curious definition of democracy that the majority making a decision is somehow tyranny and that, by implication, the minority should have the right either to make the decision or to see that no decision will be made.
I can quote one outstanding authority on this. I wish there were some Liberals here to hear this. I can remember the former Liberal Prime Minister, Mr. Trudeau, objecting that after a reasonable period of debate there should be an opportunity for the House to make a decision, there should be an opportunity for a vote to be taken.

It is right that members of the Opposition should have time in which to make criticisms and constructive suggestions. Speech:
Mr. Speaker, it is correct that we have suggested there be additional spending in many areas, areas which we believe would stimulate the economy because it is expenditure on investment rather than expenditure on matters which will do nothing to help the economy. It will be very difficult for us as Liberals to match the side-show put on two weeks ago when the Government decided to spend $163 million in one constituency simply to win one by-election. That has been worked out to, I think, around $6,000 per elector in Lac-Saint-Jean. When the Government wants to win a byelection it starts spending money like crazy without any attention to what the outcome of the expenditure will be.
Let me say that there are areas where we must spend more money. We must do it in order to bring about social justice, and we must spend more money to stimulate the economy. The area I was talking about, training and education, is as much an investment in infrastructure of this country as investment in airports, ports, roads, and economic infrastructure. A trained work force is essential for a modern economy. To cut money in training our work force and putting people to work is complete nonsense. It is the kind of thing one cannot stop and start easily. Once it is stopped it is very difficult then to start it up and hope to bear the fruit of that start-up in a short period of time.
We all know that it takes five to six years to train an engineer after university. It takes a long time to train archaeologists, metallurgists, and so on. Trained personnel are not trained overnight. Once you cut programs for these people and they become unemployed, or there is no opportunity for young people and middle-aged people to go into these fields of work, you are left without skilled workers and professionals for a period of time. I see, in Toronto, in the area from which the Hon. Member comes, there is now a shortage of skilled workers. Of course, what happens is, we have a shortage of skilled workers in Toronto and a high rate of unemployed unskilled workers in Atlantic Canada and elsewhere.
I would submit, Mr. Speaker, not enough attention has been paid to training, employment and education in this country by this Government.

I feel that this is an experience that we have endured-and I use the word advisedly-before, in regard to the extension of the expiry date of the Customs Tariff respecting the prohibition on the import of pornographic materials and hate literature. It is a rather sad irony that we are forced to do this again, for I believe the third time, and particularly that we are forced to do so because of a judgment of the Federal Court of Appeal.
That judgment, after all, ruled on the applicability of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms. I believe that when that Charter was passed most of us thought that it would be something that could be used to protect the weaker members of our society against the sort of aggression that the importation of pornography and hate literature represents.
By the perverse machinations of the legal system it came up with a ruling that rather made it easier to import pornography and hate literature into Canada. I think that it is a sad reflection on the way in which power has been vested in the judiciary in our society and taken away from the democratically elected organs of society that we are forced to do this now again, as I said, for the third time.
I should take this opportunity to point out to Canadians and to Members of the House the very narrow distinction, if any exists, between pornography and hate literature. We in this Party believe that much of what is today termed pornography is in fact hate literature aimed at women and children and that the function of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms should be to protect society, and thus women and children, from those forms of hate literature.
Because of the striking down of provision 99210 in the Customs Tariff which prohibited, and I quote, "the importation of books, printed paper, drawings, paintings, prints, photographs or representations of any kind of a treasonable or seditious or of an immoral or indecent character", we have amended the Customs Tariff. The other reason we are amending the Customs Tariff is of course the fact that we have not had a Bill passed in this House which defines and outlaws pornography and hate literature.
My hon. friend from Saint-Jacques pointed out that simply the importation was governed by the Customs Tariff and that there was no provision in Bill C-135 that would effectively control locally produced obscene or hate propaganda materials.
The Government has been successful to a limited degree by providing a tighter definition of obscene material in the Customs Tariff. I do not believe the insertion of a sunset clause was unwise, but it is because the sunset clause and its latest reincarnation expire this weekend that we have to come forward with this motion to extend that sunset clause for 18 months, and it has to be by means of a Bill.
I sincerely hope, and I am sure all Canadians share this sentiment whatever are their views on the matter of pornography and hate literature, that within 18 months either this Government or our Government which will succeed it, will manage to bring in a workable definition of pornography and hate literature that can be widely supported within the Canadian community and can be applied not only to prevent the importation of such materials but also to prevent their local production.
By the operation of Bill C-135, obscene material according to Section 159 and hate propaganda according to Section 281.3 of the Criminal Code, always assuming the perverse and capricious other House does not interfere with the passage thereof, will be prohibited from introduction into Canada for a further 18 months.
Let us not lose sight of the objective that we should have in this House, the objective of producing a workable definition of what is pornography, what is hate literature, what is erotica, and of enshrining that definition into law so that we can safeguard Canadians, particularly women and children, from the effects of what I believe can ultimately be included in the definition of hate propaganda.

Mr. Speaker, we are here today to discuss one of the most devastating pieces of legislation ever brought before the House of Commons. We are here to debate a Bill which will finish Canada as we know it and replace it with a Canada that will become nothing more than a colony of the United States.
So urgent and compelling is the impatience of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) to pack up this country and ship it south that we are going to debate this Bill for only a few hours. It took 121 years for Canadians to build this Confederation. The Government is proposing to undo that in less than half that number of hours. This Bill represents over 1,000 days of intricate negotiations between the two countries. We will debate the result of those 1,000 days in five days before the House of Commons.

This Bill is a disaster like the trade agreement it will give force of law.
With this measure, the Government is telling Canadians they have no choice but to accept or reject this agreement. It is telling this House that the elected representatives of the Canadian people have no say in the drafting of this Bill and can do nothing to diminish its impact on our country.
We are being forced to pass this legislation in a matter of days without even having seen the corresponding U.S. bill.
At every stage of the talks, there were major differences of opinion between both governments about the wording and the content of the agreement. Nevertheless, this Government is now obliging us to adopt its version of the Bill without giving us a chance to examine the legislation proposed in the U.S. Congress.
Only two and a half weeks ago, the Prime Minister's Chief of Staff was still in Washington to negotiate differences between the United States and Canada, not just on minor points but on fundamental issues like the definition of subsidies.

This Bill greatly offends Canadian tradition in three ways: it is anti-parliamentary, it is anti-democratic, it is anti-Constitution. We are being presented with an omnibus Bill which changes 27 existing Acts of Parliament. Clause 8 commits us never again to pass a statute inconsistent with this Bill, never again to enact legislation inconsistent with this trade deal. The
Bill is to supersede any other Act of Parliament, past or future. It has almost the authority of a constitutional provision. Yet the discussion draft that the U.S. Congress negotiated between the U.S. Senate and the House of Representatives indicates that that version of the trade Bill, the American version of the trade Bill, can be amended by any subsequent Act of Congress. Not only that, we find that Canadians can be fined, even imprisoned, for contravening American law, present and future, laws we haven't even seen yet.
I raised this in the House of Commons. The Minister was surprised. Now we know why. He has not read the whole deal. He has not studied the document. I am going to take him and the House through several of the provisions that relate right to the fundamental nature of our country. I doubt that the government Members read any of the Bill at all. Here is what it says about people who do not uphold the trade agreement as incorporated into the Bill.
Section 77.26 (1)-Every person who contravenes or fails to comply with ... (C) a protective order covering business proprietary and other privileged information made under American law ... is guilty of offence and is liable ... (E) on conviction and indictment, to a fine not exceeding one million dollars.
The Bill before this House involves Canadians in potential liability, potential imprisonment, and fines up to $1 million, not for offending Canadian law, not for contravening Canadian regulation, but for offending American law, present or future, laws that have not yet been enacted by the U.S. Congress. The Bill is anti-parliamentary for those reasons, and it is also anti-democratic.
Turning to public hearings, we do not know whether the committee will allow public hearings. There have been no public hearings on this Bill to date. There were no public hearings allowed on the text of the agreement. The only hearings across the country were on the general principles of that agreement. There has been no opportunity for Canadians publicly, before their elected representatives or Members of Parliament, to analyse the deal, to make their points, their submissions, to present their briefs on the deal, to analyse the real impact of the deal on their lives, their unions, their jobs, their professions, their businesses.
The whole procedure has been anti-democratic. The Prime Minister has no mandate for this legislation. It alters the fundamental direction of Canada. There was no mention of it in the last general election. It was not a theme put before the people of Canada in the last election. The only time Canadians were ever given an inkling, given an understanding of the Prime Minister's view on this very fundamental issue was when he sought the leadership of the Conservative Party at its national convention in 1983, and when, in response to a debate with the current Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson), the current Minister for International Trade (Mr. Crosbie), the current Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark), he was asked what he thought about free trade and his words were
June 29, 1988

quite clear. "Free trade," he said, "it affects our sovereignty, and we will have none of it."
Those were the words of the Prime Minister when it suited him to be against free trade. Our Prime Minister's aversion to sticking to his word has become famous. Some would say even legendary.
Canadians were not consulted nor did they authorize a deal which changes the whole direction of Canadian history, and we need an election so that Canadians can decide.

We are concerned, Mr. Speaker, about maintaining our national personality. We are concerned with maintaining our national integrity, our cultural identity, control over our resources, our economy, our social programs, and our regional development programs-no north and south division as in the United Kingdom. Ours is a country where there is equality of opportunity from the Atlantic to the Pacific to the northern Arctic. We are concerned over our ability to set an independent foreign policy. These are the issues at stake.
Mr. Speaker, from the very beginning of these talks, the Government tried to convince us that we were examining a free trade agreement. That is a myth that should be laid to rest once and for all. In spite of its title and the Government's definitions, this agreement is not free trade.
I also think we should avoid getting into the debate about whether we are for or against the philosophy of free trade, we in the Liberal Party have always been in favour of freer trade, of liberalizing trade and reducing tariff barriers. What we are discussing today is not free trade. It is a selective trade agreement. A number of industries are included and a number are excluded. We must analyse the FTA like any other contract. What did we gain and what did we lose? What did we get and what did we give away?
But read it! Whatever I go in Canada, I tell Canadians: Read the text. And now I have to say the same thing to the Minister: Read the document, sir.
This is not free trade. And it is an agreement that is costing us a pretty penny. We are paying the price every day ...

If it were just a matter of lowering trade barriers, lowering tariffs, we as a Party have always been in favour of that, always in favour of broadening our commerce. We have to remind the House and the country that 80 per cent of all the transactions that now move across the Canadian-American border either way go forward free of tariff. We succeeded under successive Liberal administrations since the War in achieving that. All we are talking about is the remaining 20 per cent, and for that remaining 20 per cent, this Prime Minister gave away the store.

Madam Speaker, although we just voted on a motion for time allocation, I think we should ask ourselves why the Government decided to limit debate in this way. Maybe that is why the Governmment wants to push this legislation through the House. We are told, Madam Speaker, that since the Second World War, customs duty dropped from an average of 20 per cent to an average of 9 per cent. We also know that 80 per cent of our trade with the United States is duty free, and that the average duty on the remaining 20 per cent is 9 per cent. So why is the Government rushing to sign an agreement for which it received no mandate? In fact, when he was Leader of the Opposition, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) said it would be unwise for Canada to sign an agreement with the United States. He used the metaphor of the mouse that gets in bed with an elephant. It could be a crushing experience!
July 4, 1988

Today we heard we shouldn't be afraid of the Americans. We should get together and trade and do business with them. Of course we shouldn't be afraid of the Americans. I believe that we as Canadians have enough maturity to take care of ourselves, without clinging to the coattails of the Americans. We shouldn't be afraid of the Americans, but, Madam Speaker, we should not get so close that our identity might be threatened. And I am afraid that this agreement could be a definite threat to our Canadian identity. There lies the danger.
Today we heard Hon. Members comparing the Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement to the European Common Market. I don't think we can draw a parallel between the two. It's like comparing apples and oranges. We have a population of 25 million in Canada, while the Americans have ten times that: 250 million. It is indeed an opportunity to be run over and swallowed up. That is where the parallel ends; there is no possible comparison with the European Common Market.
When this agreement was discussed, Canadians were assured that there was no question of signing it unless some concessions were obtained from the Americans. First was guaranteed access to the U.S. market of 250 million consumers. We were also promised, we were told that there would be a commission to settle trade disputes between the two countries. People are trying to have us believe that the agreement gives us guaranteed access to the American market. But I cannot find this guarantee anywhere in the agreement. Access to the U.S. market will only be guaranteed if Canadians produce high quality goods at competitive prices. That is what gives us guaranteed access; the agreement will not be able to do that.
We could talk for a long time about the binational commission. It exists, it is there in the agreement. But unfortunately, this commission has no power except to see whether the countervailing measures sought comply with the law of the country concerned. If so, the commission can do absolutely nothing about it! We are not exempt from duties imposed by American laws.
During the debate, we also said that the Province of New Brunswick supported this free trade agreement. I will point out to you, Madam Speaker, that the Premier of New Brunswick, Mr. McKenna, nevertheless set some conditions, which have not yet been met.

A second condition is that Canada no longer be subject to protectionist measures. The omnibus bill is still alive and has not been dealt with. So, Madam Speaker, this condition has not been met.

Madam Speaker, I have a strong interest in the matter raised by the Hon. Member for Kamloops-Shuswap (Mr. Riis). As a member of the Finance Committee I participated in our investigation into the situation of the Canadian Commercial and Northland Banks. I also participated with that committee in our study of the regulation of financial institutions. Approximately two years ago we issued a report which included major recommendations in that area. Subsequently the Government has moved in a legislative sense on most of those recommendations, not always completely in agreement, but addressing all the areas of concern.
One of the problems is that the federal Government does not have complete jurisdiction in this area. Essentially, this motion is suggesting that the Government should consider the advisability of co-operating with the provinces. There has never been any lack of intent to co-operate with the provinces in achieving the intent of this motion. The Minister of State for Finance (Mr. Hockin) has been attempting to do that. I suppose that is one of the difficulties of the federal system, but it is heightened in a system where people do not necessarily know under what rules the institution may be operating.
In large measure the motion has been triggered by the collapse of the Principal Group, with which I am familiar because it is resident in my own city. I might mention that none of the 127 companies associated with the Principal Group were federally registered. In fact, only one company, Principal Savings and Trust, was CDIC insured. I would suggest that if the Principal Group had been federally registered, none of those problems would have occurred, because in large measure those problems were the result of or compounded by what is referred to as "self-dealing" which are transactions between related companies. Many of those transactions would not have been allowed under the proposals put forward by the Finance Committee in the new legislation, or even under the existing legislation.
When the CCB and the Northland Bank collapsed, the federal Government paid insured depositors, as was required under the CDIC Act, and it also acted to reimburse insured depositors for two reasons. One, it felt there was an element of fairness required to reimburse those people. The Government had indicated that it wanted to see those banks continue, and that it wanted to play a part. Therefore, to some degree the Government was a partner in continuing those institutions prior to their collapse. Second, in paying out more than $1 billion to uninsured depositors, the federal Government recognized that at that time the economy of western Canada, particularly Alberta, could not stand the blow of losing $1 billion.

Thank you, Madam Speaker, if I have referred to a member absent from the House, I made a mistake. I wanted to refer to the silence of the Secretary of State on this matter and to the fact that the government seems to be tolerating the behaviour of some of its important members, and even some of its ministers, allowing them to take a stand against a basic policy of the government.
Madam Speaker, our time is limited, but I would also like to mention an issue which seems to be of concern to Canadians, the problems facing the language teachers who have now been on strike or locked out for a period of eight to nine months,
Official Languages Act
who are being asked by the Treasury Board to work five more hours a week and who would see their capability to teach in both official languages diminished. The four amendments in front of us do not directly, but indirectly, relate to that clause. The member for Ottawa-Vanier (Mr. Gauthier) wants to know if we think the Act must ensure the strenghtening of the equal status of both languages, Madam Speaker, and that is a very important matter. On the one hand, the government says he is for the official languages principle, but, on the other hand, he does nothing to implement this principle and does not react to the concerns of the French speaking community, and of Quebeckers. But when the defender of the rights of the French-speaking Canadians, the new minister who has just joined us, keeps quiet on this issue, I think we are entitled to ask ourselves some questions and to feel concerned, Madam Speaker.

I just want to say, finally, that in the committee a substantial number of adjustments and changes were made to this Bill. They were made in an effort to try to accommodate some of the concerns that have been expressed by different Members, including some constituents in my riding of Ottawa Centre, and there was an honest effort at compromise and in finding constructive solutions to the concerns being expressed by members from the Conservative back benches and from time to time by constituents of mine in Ottawa Centre or elsewhere.
To come at the last minute with this lengthy series of amendments, which at one time or another suggested that the Armed Forces should be English only, that the National Capital Region's language of work should be English, that the basic commitment to bilingualism should be reversed or should be undermined, at a time when we know that it is fundamental to our country and fundamental to keeping the country together, is not playing fair.
I hope that Canadians who are watching this debate realize what we are talking about here. This began as an effort by the Government, I believe, to reinforce the principle of official bilingualism. Unfortunately, it has turned into a sorry and distressing and regrettable affair in which one is forced to question the commitment of the Government to the concept and principle of bilingualism because of the degree to which they have allowed two messages to go out.
When the Member for Winnipeg-Assiniboine (Mr. McKenzie) presents himself in the election next time, will he be supporting the Government's policy of bilingualism or will he in fact be against? No matter how he votes tonight or how he votes tomorrow, a Parliamentary Secretary, without being disciplined, will have been allowed to have raised serious questions which indicate that he is not at all in sympathy with the basic tenet of government policy, and that I believe to be unacceptable.
I think I would apply the same comments to one of the ViceChairmen of the Standing Joint Committee on Official Languages, who is another of this group of 15 back-benchers


Official Languages Act
opposed to bilingualism. I think he too, particularly since the position is that of the vice-chairmanship of the Official Languages Committee, should retire himself from those particular functions.
As far as back-benchers are concerned, Madam Speaker, I am not sure whether or not they could be disciplined without being kicked out of the caucus. I think, however, that the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and the Secretary of State (Mr. Bouchard), who is responsible for bilingualism, should surely by now in a week have been able to stand up and say directly, not indirectly, that they did not agree and that they condemn those interventions which are so harmful to the Party, to our Parliament and to this country.

BasePK: 3744611

Speech:
Madam Speaker, I am pleased to take part today in the debate on Bill C-72, especially after my colleague the Minister of Justice (Mr. Hnatyshyn) and also the Hon. Member for Charlevoix (Mr. Hamelin). I think that all Members in this House will recognize the tremendous work done by that man over a little more than a year on Bill C-72. Thanks to him the legislation came through as it now stands and as it looks acceptable to us of course, without the amendments moved.
The matter could be dealt with under various angles, Madam Speaker. We could look for various reasons to take heart, point to various aspects showing that the Bill is a tremendous step forward in the recognition of our Canadian language duality, not only for Francophones but also for Anglophones and all Canadians in this country.
I think the essential feature or one of the essential features of the Canadian reality is its bilingual and multicultural nature. And when dealing with Bill C-72, it is fitting in my view that we remember all those who before us, often in the face of great difficulty, and the last time having been in 1969, worked for the official recognition of both languages. It is my view that the country they built, Madam Speaker, holds a very special place in the world thanks to its features, especially its language features.
It is my personal view that courage and determination are needed to build a country, develop it and to give it a greater degree of security and prosperity than we ourselves enjoyed. But more is needed-generosity and also, today especially, Madam Speaker, tolerance. Nothing durable survived in this country unless it was two-dimensional, with the co-operation and above all the respect of both communities.

There is not and there cannot be in Canada only one language or only one culture. There cannot be only one way of doing things, of saying or thinking things in Canada. I could say more. But there must always be only one objective for all Canadians: the unity and the prosperity of this country. The official linguistic minorities in Canada are well aware that the battle for justice and equity is a long one and that it is not over
yet. It will not be won by any glorious action, nor will it be won by a long constitutional or political battle.
The battle will be long because it deals with issues that are emotional for all Canadians. We can all say to each other here that by voting for Bill C-72 we will have progressed in the cause for linguistic justice in Canada.
[ Translation]
Madam Speaker, it is important to state here, as I feel I have a duty to do so, in what context we have to deal with amendments to Bill C-72, and my wish is to do so with the least possible degree of frustration and emotion. But it is extremely difficult for a French-speaking Member of this House, whose forebears for 350 years fought for the recognition of one's language, to try and understand why someone might wish through a series of amendments to weaken, slow down and even paralyze in certain circumstances the development of a bilingual Canada.
I think that attempt can only be understood by referring to attitudes and concepts that were more in use in this country some 20 years ago, but no longer appear to reflect Canadian realities. In my opinion, this shows that by updating this legislation which dates back to 1969, this Conservative Government has the courage and the will to make the defense of linguistic rights and cultural minorities priority in its approach to the future.
Madam Speaker, I suggest it is very important... I feel I am a richer man today for having had the opportunity over the past four years to learn another language. I must admit it was not always easy.

English has been the key that has permitted me to discover a new country, a new Canada. I have many good friends in places that I did not know existed not too long ago.
I am trying to say that we must not see bilingualism as the only means by which we will give justice to our official linguistic minorities, important as that may be. I think the younger generations of Canadians today all over the country- which is the wonderful part of the new Canada- have shown us something. I had the experience as the Secretary of State of travelling back and forth across the nation two years ago and saw how our young Canadians have taught us that bilingualism is, in fact, an opportunity for our personal and collective development.
There is not a more obvious proof of this new spirit and tolerance than the Meech Lake Accord concluded between all the Canadian provinces and the federal Government. I recognize that Quebec constitutes a distinct society within Canada and the linguistic duality is a fundamental distinction that we must protect. This Accord did not happen overnight. This Accord exists because it was inspired by realism, because


Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement
it took into consideration the real nature of Quebec and of Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I am going to speak to this Bill very briefly as one who has had personal experience with an allergic reaction which necessitated my going to the hospital on three occasions, twice here in the national capital area, in fact to the Riverside Hospital, and once in Nairobi, Africa, where I took a severe allergic reaction to some foods that 1 had eaten. One instance, in fact, caused me to go into a very difficult breathing period when I thought I was going to pass out and die. I can relate very closely to this Bill from a personal point of view.
The Bill is entitled Bill C-289, an Act to amend the Food and Drugs Act. This Bill is designed to help Canadians with food allergies when they eat out at restaurants or places that supply fast foods. As you know, Sir, there are many within our country. We had a very unfortunate incident recently in which a young lady in the National Capital Region died from an
Food and Drugs Act
allergic reaction to some nuts that she ate which she did not realize were in the food she had consumed.
The particular Bill here would have a dual effect. First, it would require every restaurant to make available for the public consultation, a list in English and French, of all the ingredients in any foods sold by it. The Bill would also compel each branch restaurant of a restaurant chain to affix on the packaging of any foods sold by it a list in English and in French of the ingredients in such food.
Many thousands of Canadians suffer from food allergies. They are described in some contexts as a nuisance. I guess I can describe my own as a nuisance because it did not persist for very long. However, for some Canadians they can be much greater than a nuisance, they can be deadly.
The CBC reported quite recently that in the last two years upward of 24 persons have died in Canada from severe allergies to foods. As things now stand, while most packaged foods sold in food stores have labelling requirements for ingredients and quantities, there are as yet no mandatory labelling requirements for restaurant food. Instead, individuals with food allergies have to ask the appropriate questions as to whether the ingredients in a restaurant food will trigger an allergic reaction. In other words, it is incumbent upon the person who goes to a restaurant to eat to ask those questions.
Therefore this Bill is performing a very valuable service in so far as it is causing a much greater debate on the subject, and in that it is raising the question of whether or not the present system is adequate. Certainly, Canadian consumers deserve the best possible protection, whether they buy food in a supermarket for preparation and consumption at home or whether they go out and eat in a restaurant, be that restaurant a very humble one or a very luxurious one.

I hope that in due course the House will do the same thing.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to propose to the House today, on behalf of the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Masse), a package of amendments to Bill C-75 dealing with an issue of deep concern to Nova Scotians, the protection of the Georges Bank fishery.
There is no dispute that the Georges Bank fishery is an important economic resource for Canada, the Province of Nova Scotia, and the people of southwestern Nova Scotia in particular.
The Government was fully aware of the importance of the Georges Bank fishery. It was also very much aware of the environmental sensitivity of the Bank and of the concerns being expressed by the Government of Nova Scotia and by the people of region over the potential impact that petroleum activity could have on the Bank. Therefore, discussions were held with the Energy Minister and the Premier of Nova Scotia and others on how best to satisfactorily resolve the impasse.
It was agreed, following these extensive discussions and consultations, that there should be a full and open public review of the environmental and socio-economic issues related to petroleum activities on the Georges Bank.
There had also been the concern expressed that such an environmental review conducted under the auspices of the Oil and Gas Management Board would not provide the objectivity this important issue deserved. As a result, it was agreed that the review would be conducted by an independent panel rather than the new Offshore Oil and Gas Management Board.

July 7, 1988

The Georges Bank is a unique fishery resource, and unique measures are required in the circumstances to balance the interests of all concerned. The moratorium and public review process will provide assurances to all Canadians that the Government understands the seriousness of environmental concerns and how these relate to other major considerations in our lives.
An agreement was reached with the Government of Nova Scotia on an amendment package for Georges Bank which contains the following key provisions. First, a moratorium is to be put in place on oil and gas activity on the Georges Bank until at least the year 2000.
Second, prior to the year 1996 an independent review panel will be constituted to hold public hearings on the environmental and social impacts of drilling on the Bank. The panel will report to the federal and provincial Ministers of Energy on or before July 1, 1999. The Ministers will then jointly decide whether the ban on petroleum activity should be extended beyond January 1, 2000.
These amendments will bring the federal accord legislation into line with that of the Province of Nova Scotia whose legislature passed the Georges Bank amendment package on May 25, 1988. The decisions embodied in the Georges Bank amendment package represent a credible solution to a very sensitive issue, one which is widely supported as being in the best public interest. I am pleased that the Governments of Canada and Nova Scotia, working together in a climate of cooperation, were able to resolve this issue.
I am today asking this House to join with others in supporting these measures by giving the amendments its stamp of approval.
