Madam Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to speak on this particular Bill. It is an area with respect to which I am not particularly well informed. However, there is a principle here which needs to be considered.
I have often wondered why it is that we think that all our non-renewable resources have to be spent as quickly as possible. That idea is the position that has been taken by much of the world's oil industry. It has been taken all over the world and, to a great extent, it has been supported by Governments around the world. In this case, the interest of companies in the Georges Bank and the development of the industry in that area ended up in a rather bitter fight between the oil exploiters and the fishermen of Georges Bank. It is good to know that in this particular situation a good look was taken at the responsibilities and the needs of both groups.
A moratorium is being imposed which gives both groups the opportunity to assure themselves that one will not hurt the other in any way when, sometime in the future, there is the possibility of development of the industry on Georges Bank. There are several attractive features in the plan which are being developed in this particular Bill by the Minister. These are positions which might be models for the future.
July 7, 1988

The previous Liberal Government took a similar type of approach in looking at the Mackenzie Valley as a source of gas and a pipeline which would have traversed all of Canada. It ended up making a recommendation, and following the recommendation which put that particular pipeline on hold. As it happens, the events have caught up to the pipeline. It now seems much less of an economic requirement. This might happen in the case of the Georges Bank as well.
The Bill establishes a model which might be used in the future with respect to the development of other resources and other conflicts that arise between industries. It is refreshing, and 1 must say unusual, to have the will of the people override the desire of large corporations to make more money. That is exactly what this particular Bill is dealing with, the desire of the industry to exploit the gas on Georges Bank, and it is against that group of people who think that perhaps it is not worth doing so. There are other examples of the use of resources to increase the value and the standard of living of part of the population. In some cases, that type of use of resources becomes worth-while. In other cases, development of resources can go in the opposite direction and do more harm to the population than good.
For example, in the development of its North Sea oil, Norway decided that the speed of development should be at the requirement of the country rather than at the requirement of the oil industry. Norway set a timetable which allowed the development to the extent that it did make for a real change in the life structure of Norwegians. Norway used the benefits from those resources to improve the lifestyle of Norwegians without a boom structure. The significance of that type of approach is very important, and it needs to be looked at and perhaps it can become a model for resource development or other industrial development in certain areas.

industry has been adversely affected by massive quantities of imported goods that might suddenly flow into the country at a certain point.
Madam Speaker, when the Legislative Committee debated the Bill we broadened the clause somewhat, because the original text of the Bill used the following expression, in English: "a major proportion of domestic production". But there are several types of industries in Canada where large producers may represent 55, 60, or 65 per cent of production, and very often those major producers are controlled by national interests or, quite frequently, by nonresident shareholders. And for all sorts of reasons related to international ramifications, those large producers might object to complaints being filed with the Tribunal to ask that Tribunal to conduct an inquiry on the import of unreasonable quantities of goods or the sale of goods at unjustifiably low prices.
The result would be that domestic producers, or the smaller ones at least, would find it impossible to file their complaints with the Tribunal to ask it to investigate massive imports affecting them.

Speech:
Mr. Speaker, we have given serious consideration to this proposed amendment but we feel that given the nature of the Bill and its wording it is not necessary.
The concern that has been raised by both Hon. Members stems from representations made by concerned Indians who will be affected by this Bill. When asked for specific examples of potential conflict between Indian rights and the agreement, none were brought forward. It is dubious at best to include a general clause in the legislation where there is no specific problem to be addressed. By doing so, we would run the risk of frustrating the over-all intent of Bill C-73.
There is concern that a broad clause protecting all treaty and other rights of the Indian people of Ontario could be at odds with the terms of negotiated specific agreements. For instance, a specific agreement could provide that unsold surrendered lands now being used as municipal streets, provincial highways or other public installations, which have been occupied by non-Indians for many years, would remain as such but Indian bands would in return be adequately compensated. It is the case in this example that the rights of Indian bands to these lands come into conflict with the terms of the specific agreement. It is because of this potential conflict that we did not consider it wise to include such a general provision regarding the protection of Indian rights.
This is not to say that the agreement does not concern itself with, and that we are not concerned with, the protection of Indian rights. First, it is the case that an Indian band involved in negotiations for the purpose of arriving at a specific agreement must be satisfied that the deal is acceptable and does not unduly compromise its rights. They have that protection.
Second, several provisions of the agreement expressly state that Indian rights are not to be compromised. In particular, I want to refer to Clauses 5 and 6 of the agreement which stipulate that neither the 1986 Indian Lands Agreement nor any specific agreement negotiated thereunder will affect the validity of any treaty or surrender, and that no federal-provincial agreement concerning any letters patent will affect any rights or the recourse that any band may have against any person or lands, including the Crown or Crown lands. Furthermore, in response to the concerns that the Bill could adversely affect lands that do not enter into specific agreements, Clause 12 of the agreement states as well that the specific agreement will affect any band unless that band confirms that particular specific agreement.
I believe the concerns expressed by the Members are fully addressed in the Bill itself. Furthermore, is it necessary to state
that aboriginal rights are protected by the Constitution of this country?

I want to say that all this Parliament has to do-starting tonight-is blow the dust off the Carter Royal Commission on taxation of 1966. For the ensuing two or three years, when the
Income Tax Act and Related Acts
Government of that day refused to act, Mr. Carter, like Mr. Justice Emmett Hall, finally got angry and went public. The tragedy is that he died of cancer before his intervention in the public domain. He was unable to have the time to force the Government of that day to implement real tax reform, that a buck is a buck and no matter how you earn it, it is taxable.
He called for-and many others have called for, including members in all the political Parties-some fundamental changes to the tax system in this country.
I listened to the Hon. Member from Edmonton a few minutes ago who dredged up mythology, falsehoods and inaccuracies from 30, 40 and 50 years ago which I thought had been so thoroughly discredited that nobody, not even a Conservative, would have the gall to even raise them again. He talked about depopulation in Saskatchewan, under the CCF. Under Conservative and Liberal Governments in that province from 1923 to 1944, we lost 400,000 people. In the equivalent period, under Tommy Douglas and the CCF, we regained more than half of that number. Then, under 11 years of A1 Blakeney, our population got back up to the million mark.
No matter what the numbers are, the point is that we have always had a different social regime in our province. Even Liberals and Tories did not dare abolish programs that we have started. They have nickelled away at them, they have undermined them, they have reduced their effectiveness, they have increased the cost to consumers, but they have not dared to do away with them. It would be political suicide for them to do so, and they know it.
The costs of services that the people of Canada need and want have to be shared equitably by every taxpayer, no matter who they are or what their station in life is. Those below the poverty line must be totally exempt from the tax system. The only way that you get them to the position of paying some of their share of taxation-which they would like to do if you could get them to an income level where they would be willing and able to-is to put them to work and provide them with the services that every Canadian needs, rich or poor.
Every one of those services paid for through our tax system is shared by everyone. It is what we like to call a co-operative commonwealth. Taxes paid for services like drugs and senior citizens, housing and chronic care beds and air ambulances and telephones and power and automobile insurance and a host of other things, are essential public services. They are not businesses; they are services. I include the Post Office in that. It is not a business; it is a public service.
There are no taxpayers in this country, no citizens that I have ever heard of other than someone from the Chamber of Commerce, or from the Tories, who complain about the deficit in the Post Office. The deficit is shared by all taxpayers in the country. Their first priority is service. It should not only be priority post, it should be priority service.

July 21, 1988
Income Tax Act and Related Acts
I want to mention something since the Hon. Member for Hamilton East (Ms. Copps) was being so vitriolic about us. Under a Liberal regime toward the middle or the end of the Korean War, we had something called corporate tax deferrals. As of this day there are between S35 billion and $40 billion of unpaid corporation taxes on the books of this country. That is a debt. If you look at the annual reports of corporations whether Canadian Pacific Investments, Canadian Pacific Limited, Inco, Bell Telephone, Air Canada, CNR, you name it, it does not matter whether it is a private or a public corporation, they have hundreds of millions of dollars of deferred corporate taxes on their books carried as liabilities. But the little corner grocery store owner, the farmer and the fisherman cannot defer their taxes. Neither can we. We have to pay them. If we are late, we are charged interest.
Canadian Pacific Limited, one of my favourite friends, owes something in the order of between $1.5 billion and $2 billion in deferred corporation taxes which will never be paid. International Nickel and Bell Telephone owe that much or more. The Government of Canada has something near $40 billion in taxes receivable which will never be paid.
If the Government were to charge those corporations just the straight bank rate of interest, the Government would pick up between $3 billion and $4 billion in extra tax revenues. That is a cheap loan, at the moment it is is an interest free loan. The theory was if you let corporations defer their taxes they would invest the money in new equipment, new plants and would create more jobs. That was the theory. They did. International Nickel, Canadian Pacific and Bell got investments like you would not believe in Mexico, Chile, Indonesia and anywhere else in the world you want to go. When 3,000 men were laid off in the Sudbury area, International Nickel opened a new mine in Chile. That is where deferred taxes went. Nobody should be allowed to defer tax until they can prove that the money was invested in this country and nowhere else.

Speech:
Mr. Speaker, I would have liked to have had an opportunity to pose questions, but I understand that that is not possible right now. I want to focus on the NDP amendment, which is an amendment to the Liberals' amendment. Today we have taken some time in the House to point out the inadequacies of the Government's policy on taxation and the unfairness of the Government's approach to taxation. It is not surprising that the Liberals would be able to come up with an amendment that appears to make sense.
The Liberals are basically saying that this House opposes in principle the taxation measures of the Government because the Bill seeks to impose a tax system that first is lacking in progressivity. What is that? Progressivity simply means that those who earn little pay little in taxes and those who earn a lot would be expected to pay a lot in taxes. It means that those who can afford to pay ought to be able to pay. It is a great principle.
Second, the Liberals say that the tax system places unfair burdens on families. That is true and it ought to be stated. Third, the Liberals state that the tax system unjustly taxes middle-income earners. That as well is true, and I spoke earlier today about the very heavy tax burden that has been placed on the middle-income earners of Canada.
Fourth, the Liberals say that the new tax system is more complex than the one presently in place. Anyone who had to fill out a tax form or who had to hire someone to fill out a tax form knows that the taxation system is very complex. There is a need for simplicity as long as that simplicity leads to greater justice in the tax system.
The fifth and sixth points made by the Liberal Party are the ones that I find interesting. The Liberals say that the new tax system discourages capital formation and reduces the competitiveness of Canadian corporations. Obviously we need capital in order to have economic growth, and our firms must be competitive, so those are good points. However, that is where the Liberals stopped. Therefore, we moved an amendment adding that we oppose the Bill because the Bill fails to ensure
that corporations make a fair and regular contribution to federal tax revenues by imposing a minimum corporate tax.
We seek to complete the circle. The Liberals have indicated they are in favour of those things that will help people, such as a progressive tax system, because the burden is unjustly laid upon middle income earners. They make that point but fail to explain how the revenue loss will be made up. When they deal with the corporate side of the ledger, they deal only with the need of corporations to be competitive and a necessity for the tax system to recognize that fact. They fail to deal with the other side of the ledger, which is that if we are to relieve the tax burden on ordinary families, as they suggest in their motion, then we have to find the revenue some place.
We in this Party believe in putting the whole picture before Canadians. The place to find that revenue is from those corporations which are making profits but not now paying taxes. I understand there are some 60,000 of them. Our amendment points out that if we are to have a just tax system, if we are to give some relief to ordinary Canadian families, it will have to come from those who now get away without paying any taxes.
The Liberals fail to recognize the problem and fail to provide the solution. They criticize the Government, which is a necessary part of being in opposition, but if you want to change the situation, you must have a solution to the problems. The Liberal motion does not do that.
That is why, when I spoke earlier today, I indicated that when Canadians look for an alternative to the tax policies they have experienced over the last four years and they look to the Liberal Party, they are looking in the wrong place and they will inevitably be disillusioned.
That is why we moved this motion. The amendment introduced by the Liberal Party was only a half measure. It was like trying to take a step by lifting up your foot and forgetting to put it down again. They have identified the problem but failed to outline the solution.
We think that problems should not only be identified, they should be solved. We think what is needed is not just a change in government but a change in direction. What is needed is not only a capacity to analyse the injustices in society, but a capacity to take the action necessary to solve those injustices and bring about a better community for all Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, I take the view that it is essential for Parliament to have this debate. I believe that Canadians have a right to know what and how their legislators are thinking about this vital issue. It has been said that living itself is life's most complete treasure. We all know that there are many kinds of violence in our society, violence that robs life of that treasure of living. There is war, highway traffic accidents, dreaded diseases of many kinds, murders, and suicides, but it is chilling for me to realize that the most violent place in Canada today is not some dark side street in a decayed section of an inner city; it is, rather, the human womb.
Each year in Canada there are more than 60,000 abortions performed. I want to say that in no way can abortion be considered as merely an elective surgical procedure. It is, as former Prime Minister Trudeau once said, and I quote: "The very frightening moral decision of killing something which is living inside a person". Even Madam Justice Bertha Wilson admitted that abortion was not just a medical decision. She said that it was a profound social and ethical one as well. This was part of her recent decision that struck down the legislation on the statute books of Canada. She also said, and again I quote: "The precise point in the development of the foetus at which the state's interests in its protection becomes compelling I leave to the informed judgment of the legislature".

She does not indicate, either, by what means this protection can be granted and guaranteed. She leaves that to us. She leaves that to the Bill which will eventually have to follow the motion we are debating today. I return to my first point, that it is therefore essential that we debate this subject in Parliament.
There are some who say that we must find that middle ground on this serious social and moral issue of abortion. I think the middle ground that some people are talking about is mythical in nature. It is non-existent. I wonder, how can there be middle ground? There is life and there is death.
In 1975 Hon. Otto Lang, then Liberal Minister of Justice, said in an interview with Bruce Garvey for The Toronto Star, and I quote: "You cannot distinguish between the life of the unborn and the born, there's no biological cut-off date". I have had the privilege to listen to distinguished physicians who have confirmed and verified that point of view.
When this Parliament, once again in a free vote, made its decision on the question of capital punishment, I, for a third time as a Member of Parliament, voted for abolition. I did so because I am pro-life and anti-violence. I am not persuaded that when the state kills felons who are guilty of murder that it makes society a better or a safer or a happier place for others.
On the contrary, I took the view that state executions merely add to the sum total of violence in society and perhaps even, in a certain sense, condone violence as an acceptable means to achieve a satisfactory end. I say no. It does not work that way. The means is unacceptable and the end is unsatisfactory.
Recently I read Truman Capote's best seller of many years ago, In Cold Blood. The savage, brutal murder of an entire family in rural Kansas by two deeply disturbed young men was a story of unprovoked, irrational violence at its worse. Yet, as Capote went on to reveal the background and personalities of those two young men, by the end of the book one did not want to see them hanged. Treatment for them, yes. Full freedom, never. But death? No.

Hughson's remarks were made during a presentation to 1,200 women attending a meeting with Elaine McCoy, minister of women's issues, May 5 in Edmonton.
The volunteer-run centre is known nationally and has a 24 hour crisis telephone line to provide anonymity and easy access to counselling, Hughson said. The centre is privately funded.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to rise today to address Bill C-144, the Canada Child Care Act. As my colleague, the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp), indicated, this Bill provides for implementation of the most important component of the national strategy on child care. It responds to the child care needs of Canadians with an innovative, flexible policy that is both generous and equitable. It represents a major move forward for children, parents, and families throughout the country.
Child care is probably one of the most pressing social issues facing legislators today. This Bill reflects this Government's strong commitment to improve the quality and quantity of care in all regions of the country. The Government will spend $6.4 billion on child care over the next seven years, and another $1 billion annually after that. This is a significant response to the realities of our society today and lays the foundation for an improved quality of life for the Canadian family in the future.
As Minister of State for Indian Affairs and Northern Development, I am especially pleased that the national strategy on child care has been expanded to recognize the special needs and concerns of Indian people. Indians must be full and productive participants in society if Canada is to go into the 21st century a more mature and stronger nation. Today a wide range of federal programs and services is provided to Indians. For example, CMHC has a rural and native housing program, DRIE's native economic development program, and CEIC's native internship program.
Mr. Speaker, Indians must also have access to child care, child care that is both flexible and affordable, so that they can concentrate on their jobs and improve their quality of life. As Hon. Members are aware, despite progress made in recent years, economic conditions in Indian communities lag behind the national average. This means that the ability of an Indian family to find good child care for its children while one or both parents work can be essential to that family's well being.
I am very glad to say that as a result of this Government's initiative, some 2,000 child care spaces for Indian children will
Canada Child Care Act
be created over six years, that is, for children living on reserves.
However, creating child care spaces according to the provincial model will not resolve a specifically Indian problem. Like all Canadians, Indians are very concerned about their children's well being, and anyone who visits Indian families living on reserves will see how important children are to those families. Child care must therefore meet safety and other standards while also respecting the social and cultural traditions of the group in question, in this case the Indians.
Mr. Speaker, Indian child care in Canada is underdeveloped. Most provincial governments have been reluctant to extend their programs to Indian reserves since they are, admittedly, a federal responsibility.
Only the Province of Ontario finances Indian child care through a contribution agreement with the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development. On some reserves, bands have set up their own daycare, but such cases are few and far between.

The Government of Canada has a special relationship with Indian people living on reserves. It was in recognition of this relationship that Health and Welfare Canada, in consultation with the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development, developed the special Indian component of the national strategy on child care. This component provides for an expenditure of $60 million over six years to develop and stimulate the growth of accredited child care services on reserves. This is the first time in Canada's history that such funds have been made available specifically to serve the needs of Indian children.
Although the administrative details of this initiative are yet to be worked out, the funding schedule has been set and some basic goals and principles have been established for the program. Beginning April 1, 1989, the Government of Canada will invest $5 million in each of the first two years of the program, $10 million in each of the third and fourth years, and $15 million in each of the final two years of the program. The funds will be administered by Health and Welfare Canada with assistance from Indian Affairs and Northern Development.
This money will be used to fund a number of significant pilot projects designed to determine exactly what is needed in terms of Indian child care and how to deliver that. It is anticipated that the program will create about 2,000 child care spaces over six years. Equally as important, it will help us establish how the Indian child care system should work.

Mr. Speaker, obviously Indians will be fully consulted on the implementation of this program in their communities, as will the provinces. Since this Government came to power, we have always taken this approach, and we intend to start consultations in the very near future.

Mr. Speaker, 1 have a number of questions. I obviously do not have enough time for them, but I would like to, first of all, clarify a couple of points that the Member made. I must say that I am surprised to see this Member, whom I have a great deal of respect for, repeating some of the misinformation that the Minister himself is promoting regarding the NDP policy. First of all, does he not realize that non-profit day care, which is what we advocate, is not the same as government institutions? There could be public day care as well. We have no objection to that. I wish that he would check into that and clarify that non-profit societies are quite a different thing than government institutions. We are saying that we believe that federal money should go to child care that is not for profit. On the other hand, we are not opposed to commercial day care, providing it is self-sustaining. If parents want to use it and pay fees for it, fine. We are not saying that it should not be commercial. We are saying that it should not be supported by tax dollars. I wish he would be more clear about that.
We are also very much in favour of in-home day care. We want women in the home or people in the home to be licensed as family day care homes, so that they will have decent pay in order to have the chance for all the resources and support that they need. They will have money to get fences and everything will be prepared the way it should be. There would be good quality family day care homes, not just baby-sitting with kids plunked in front of a TV set. If parents still want to use casual informal care, that is their right. We should not be paying federal money. I wanted to clarify those points first.
I will now get to my question. The former Minister, who is well informed on matters of justice, mentioned the question of national objectives. I do not agree with what he was saying and what the Liberals keep saying about national standards. It is not the role of the federal Government to establish standards in areas that are provincial jurisdiction. This was analysed over and over again in our committee, with considerable expertise on this.
In both medicare and health and welfare, the question of standards are a provincial jurisdiction, but certainly those standards should be based on principles. I would ask him to clarify a little bit more the significance of not having national objectives. Also, does he feel, as I do, that the Government seems to be trying to push this particular social program-the only new social program that we have had for many, many years-through before Meech Lake is applied, and has deliberately not put in "the national objectives", which would be required under the Meech Lake Accord?
There is no statement of principles on which provinces would be required to base their standards. There is also no enforcement mechanism as we have in medicare. I wonder if he would comment further on that and if he has any suggestions as to how this should be developed in a way that is closer to the medicare model.

He said: Mr. Speaker, it gives me great pleasure to rise to speak briefly on this very important Bill and the amendment which I tabled two days ago. I want to explain some of the reasons why this amendment was tabled and why this Bill is very important.

However, we abdicate our responsibility and duty by allowing contradictory messages to be sent to the youth of the nation by allowing head shops or drug paraphernalia outlets to sell their products, such as hookah pipes to the youth, the most important resource that we have in Canada.

The Canadian Pharmaceutical Association was concerned that under this Bill, as it was reported from committee, drug stores could be convicted of selling or giving hypodermic needles and syringes to diabetics. The Canadian Medical Association was concerned that if these hypodermic needles and syringes were obtained by someone claiming to be a diabetic who was actually a drug addict, it could promote the spread of AIDS.

Interpretation
"United States" means
(a)	the customs territory of the United States, including the fifty states of the United States, the District of Columbia and Puerto Rico,
(b)	the foreign trade zones located in the United States and Puerto Rico, and

Speech:
Madam Speaker, as we are all aware, it is the official mandate of certain Departments to be concerned with the health of Canadians. Together, the Department of National Health and Welfare and the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs work to ensure the development and adoption of legislation designed to protect the Canadian consumer, keep Canadians informed, and ensure their fundamental well-being. It is in that same spirit that the Food and Drug Act regulates the labelling of drugs to ensure that users are aware of the quantities of all medicinal ingredients in those products.
Similar rules are also applied to the packaging and labelling of numerous consumer products that Canadians purchase in grocery stores and put on the dinner table every day. It is not only a matter of ensuring that Canadians eat well and take safe and effective medical products when they are needed, but of respecting their right to be well and properly informed about what they consume. Further, it is a matter of making it possible for those who suffer from allergies to know precisely what substances and ingredients make up the drugs they take and the foods they eat.
Bill C-289 directly addresses the concerns of those Canadians who may unwittingly consume foods containing specific ingredients to which they are allergic or whole foods that bring on allergic reactions.
Under the provisions of this legislation restaurateurs would have to make available to their clientele a list of all ingredients used in the preparation of the foods offered on their menus. Similarly, restaurant franchises and chains would have to list the ingredients they use on their product packaging. Of course, Madam Speaker, this should be done in both official languages.
Let me expand upon this matter further in order to show clearly that the problem addressed by Bill C-289 is of real and pressing concern. For example, diabetics and those suffering from celiac disease must exercise great care in finding out the ingredients of all foods which they themselves have not prepared. If in doubt, these people must simply avoid the food product.
The same holds true for those who suffer from food-related allergies. They must be ever cautious in asking restaurants for complete details on the ingredients and makeup of the food in the meals being offered. For people in both these categories, as well as for many others too numerous to mention here today, it often comes down to their very survival, a matter of life and death.
Since October, 1986, at least three people have died as a result of allergic reactions brought on by foods eaten in restaurants where the ingredients were not known to them. Of those, two were teenagers. Had better and more complete information been available, these tragedies might not have occurred.
It is true that the concept of allergic reaction and its relationship to food is, in most cases, poorly defined. We are all aware that certain foods and certain drinks may lead to upset digestion or allergic reactions and that these reactions, although fortunately mild for the most part, are nonetheless unpleasant.
We also know that the effects of these same irritants can be exacerbated when we are worried, over-tired, ill, or subject to great stress. Finally, we know that in facing all these allergic reactions the medical community seems singularly perplexed and at a loss when it comes to quantifying the incidence, gravity, and growth of these problems. Certainly science is evolving rapidly along with new and improved techniques and we remain hopeful that effective solutions will be found.
However, we must take steps to avoid the death of other children who may suffer for simply having a snack after a hockey game, a swim meet, or a general get together. So, too, we must act on behalf of those consumers who, for reasons medical, religious, or personal, must avoid certain foods or ingredients and be made aware of their presence. We can no longer remain indifferent.
It should also be noted that the foods we eat today undergo complex processing and are made up of numerous ingredients. Most restaurants make use of an incredible number of ingredients in preparing their products. Even those establishments with limited menus and fast food outlets can use up to 1,000 ingredients. In the vast majority of cases these restaurants are at the mercy of suppliers who themselves can alter and substitute ingredients without notice.
Faced with the complexity of this situation, something must be done. We must determine the nature of the problem from a medical standpoint; identify the allergies, the foods involved, the groups exposed, and the treatment for those who suffer; and carry out the necessary research. We must increase awareness within the restaurant industry in order that its members can fulfil their duty to advise the public as to the ingredients they employ. Finally, we must protect the health of all Canadians who are vulnerable and who need not take chances when dining in restaurants.
As a result of Bill C-289 we have the chance to take a step in the right direction by proposing a solution, however imperfect it may be. I am convinced that the authorities within the Departments of National Health and Welfare and Consumer and Corporate Affairs will undertake a detailed examination of all that it entails and continue to ensure the safety of Canadians so that they will be able to enjoy eating outside the home without fear of allergic reaction.
August 19, 1988

Speech:
Madam Speaker, I am happy to have the opportunity to participate in private Members' hour and in the consideration of Bill C-289 which is a proposed Act to amend the Food and Drugs Act and concerns the listing of ingredients contained in restaurant food. The Bill would compel every restaurant to make available to the public a list, in English or in French, of all the ingredients in any food it sells.
This is certainly a sensitive issue that has received a great deal of attention from health professionals, food regulators, the media and the public at large. Certainly this attention is well justified. Tragic deaths have resulted from allergic reactions to restaurant food, particularly in so-called fast-food restaurants. According to various news reports, some 25,000 Canadians are at risk every day because of their food allergies, and some 24 people have died in Canada over the past two years alone because of allergic reactions to food eaten in restaurants.
It is heartening to note that the Minister of National Elealth and Welfare (Mr. Epp) is well aware of this problem. I had the pleasure of attending a committee meeting at which he was present and at which this issue was discussed. The Minister is also very concerned about this problem. He has already issued instructions to his Department to determine how much if any of an increase in food sensitivity reactions there has been, whether a perceived increase might be due to the availability of better instrumentation and diagnosis and whether the population as a whole is becoming more sensitive for one reason or another. Certainly the media attention that has focused on this issue in the last year or so could be a factor in that.
In addition, the House of Commons Standing Committee on Health and Welfare has held hearings, one of which I was present at, on the feasibility of mandatory labelling for food products sold in restaurants and fast food outlets. The Government is determined to find the best solution to the problem. It is likely that a large proportion of food sensitivity reactions are linked to relatively few foods or food components. On the other hand, almost any food has the potential to trigger a serious allergic reaction in a particular individual who is perhaps more than generally sensitive.
This problem is complex, and it is vital, therefore, to solicit input from all parties concerned. Officials from Health and Welfare Canada and from the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs have consulted with both the Canadian Food and Restaurant Association and the Allergy Information Association. Consensus has been reached that a chart identifying foods served in an establishment and an indication as to whether or not they contain substances for listing on a so-called priority list was perhaps the most suitable mechanism for providing the information required by consumers with food sensitivities.
In this context, I think it is appropriate to quote from a letter from Mr. Douglas Needham, Executive Vice President
Food and Drugs Act
of the Canadian Restaurant and Food Services Association. Mr. Needham writes that his association:
-supports the consumer's right to know the ingredients used in restaurant
meals, and that his Association continues to work with all concerned groups
to identify and implement measures that will decrease the likelihood of more
tragic deaths.
I think Mr. Needham and his association should be applauded for that stand.
In fact, according to a recent report by the Canadian Press, the Canadian Restaurant and Food Services Association is strongly encouraging a voluntary program among its 6,800 members. Industry spokespeople such as Mr. Needham have said that restaurant menus should warn consumers of ingredients that could lead to allergic reactions before they order meals. The association has suggested a system of warning charts that could be introduced in quick service restaurant chains because these establishments have a highly centralized control over ingredients.
The consistency of the menus in chain restaurants combined with the limited choices that are normally available make the charts a manageable idea. According to the same report by Canadian Press, the association has talked with 24 quick service or fast food restaurant chains, and of those 24, 22 have voluntarily agreed to take part in such a plan. This is good news. It shows that the food industry is well aware of the problem and is more than willing to take some steps to resolve it. It further shows that the idea of an ingredients list, if it can be adequately fine tuned and made manageable and practical, is indeed a good one.
It is quite possible that the best way to protect Canadians with food allergies as they dine out is through the use of an ingredients list. If this is the case, then every effort should be made to adopt the very best listing system possible. In this light, it seems quite probable that Bill C-289, effective as it has been in focusing attention on the problem, can be improved. It is essential that consumers get the information they need to protect themselves in the market-place and to make intelligent choices. This applies as much to allergy sufferers who dine in restaurants as it does to anyone else.
The Government is determined to bring about an effective solution to this issue. If that solution is found to centre upon ingredient disclosure lists, then the House can be assured that the listing requirements will be applied in a manner that is effective, fair and as cost-efficient as possible.

One of the claims by the current Conservative Government in support of a trade deal with the U.S. is that what was going on under the American law took too long. Instead under the GATT the panel set up to look into disputes about the proper application of American law or other member countries' laws could say whether those laws were proper in light of the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade itself. If the panel said they were not, then those laws could not be applied.
This treaty takes away the right of the Canadian Government to go to GATT on behalf of Canadian exporters to the United States. The debate this evening is certainly a hallmark in history when Members of Parliament rise to see who can outdo whom, and who loves children and mothers the most. Members that opposing this Bill seems to be against motherhood, against children, and against choice, I seem to be in very good company. This association, many of whom are women, but who are a cross-section of people, have stated that this Bill ignores the child care needs of Canadian families, and does not encourage the development of a national child care system. They also acknowledge that child care is an issue of national importance and deserves the full public scrutiny available through the legislative process. Organizations that have joined in this letter to the Prime Minister include the National Action Committee

He stated: "This would be a better world for children if parents had to eat the spinach".
I would suggest that if the Prime Minister and his colleagues had to utilize low-quality child care, deal with constantly revolving child caregivers, inadequate child care spaces and facilities, and be forced to pay high child care costs, we may have a very different child care Act before us, and indeed a better world for children.
Other speakers today have stated that, in their constituency, 85 per cent of their constituents are happy with the choices which they have to utilize the child care of their choice. In reviewing how far this Bill will take us in addressing the real crisis, I have to say that in sum this Bill is simply an articulate voice of the past.

Many of the arguments put forth tonight about child care in general were arguments that were raised in those debates about public education. As the previous speaker so aptly said, we are not exactly saying that child care will be analogous to the public education system, but there are certain principles which are being advocated, just as were done in the public education system. Those are principles of national standards in order that Canadians and their children from coast to coast will have affordable, accessible child care.

If adopted, Motion No. 3 would, first of all, transform the deduction into a tax credit. We know that currently, the deduction is $2,000. This Bill will raise the deduction to $4,000 for children up to the age of 6, but only for families who provide receipts. If you hire someone and you have receipts for child care expenses, you can deduct up to $4,000 annually for children up to the age of 6. Before, there was a maximum of $8,000 per family. That will disappear. We know that a family that incurs child care expenses but does not have receipts, or where one of the spouses stays home to look after the children, can obtain a maximum increase of $200 annually of the refundable child tax credit. However, this applies only to families on lower incomes.

But regarding the expense deduction, we believe that it would be preferable to have some consistency and keep the tax credit approach as much as possible. And since it is a tax credit that helps families, we believe that this tax credit applicable to child care expenses should be 26 per cent. For example, a family with $2,000 in child care expenses would be entitled to a tax credit of 26 per cent of $2,000; if it has $4,000 in child care expenses, it would be entitled to a tax credit of 26 per cent. That is my proposal. It does not change the ceiling, but simply changes the deduction into a proportional tax credit. Why 26 per cent? Because it would help families with modest incomes more. Under the present tax reform, their income is taxed at 17 per cent. The first $27,500 of refundable income and a 26 per cent tax credit would thus benefit families making $27,500 or less and would change nothing, or very little, for families with more substantial incomes.

So I make this proposal for two purposes: first, to keep some consistency in the use of tax credits, since the Government has decided to eliminate exemptions and to change them into tax credits, 1 do not see why this should not be done for child care expenses; second, it would enable families with child care expenses who are in the lowest income bracket to obtain a 26 per cent tax credit for them.

Madam Speaker, I intended to start out by saying that I had been thinking a lot about this speech, during the long, interminable set of speeches by both the Government and the Official Opposition. I say this seriously, too, because despite the duress of closure having been used by the Government, despite what we might call the dirty tricks of millions of dollars of advertising being spent to try to promote the trade deal, there is still a fundamental choice, a basic debate that faces Canada. I think that it is very much, when we get right down to it, a question of direction and philosophy. On one hand we have belief in basically unrestricted capitalism, a society which is driven by profit, by the fast buck, where those who own our large corporations basically call the shots, and where that is justified by the fact that they are believed to drive the economy forward.
The United States has always been the greatest example in the world of that kind of society of unrestricted capitalism in which the search for profit has driven what has taken place. It is for people who believe this view of the world. It is not a minus in any sense to integrate into the United States. On the contrary, it is a giant plus, because they see themselves as tying into an economy which is itself the model of that unrestricted capitalism.
On the other hand, there is a belief in people before profit, a belief in community, where we can take care of each other, where we share power instead of seeing that power concentrated in large corporations, in large organizations, and in large government. It is not so much a view that unrestricted capitalism does not work, though I think it is pretty clear, looking at the last 100 years, that unrestricted capitalism does not work successfully. Governments have to intervene. They have to smooth out business cycles. They have to provide infrastructure for the large corporate sector to make the money which drives it forward.
As I said, it is not so much a view that this unrestricted capitalism does not work; it is a much more positive view. It is a view that sees human beings fulfilled as people by much, much more than money, by much, much more than profit. It sees them fulfilled in a fair, caring and sharing society. That is the different perspective from which we in our Party approach this trade deal.
The fact is that this deal stops us from being able to build in the future that kind of fair, caring and sharing society for average families for which we as a Party have always fought. That is why we fight so strongly and will continue to do so as long as we possibly can. That is what it is all about.
When we cut through the rhetoric, the false statistics that are thrown out by the Minister for International Trade (Mr. Crosbie), the nonsense which the Minister spoke in much of his speech, that is what it is all about. It is a question of direction: Do we choose the direction of unrestricted capitalism, U.S. style, or do we choose the chance to build a caring, fair society for average families in which they will have power to shape their lives? That is what it is all about.
This deal is in fact the biggest hoax Canadians have experienced in hundreds of years. The Government says that this is a trade deal. If we look through it, we find that there are chapters and chapters which deal with anything but trade. They deal with investment, agriculture, financial services, services themselves, emergency actions, technical standards, wine and distilled spirits. These are issues which are important to the people within those sectors. They are important to us as we try to shape monetary policy for our country. They are far, far more than a trade deal. Yet that is what we find throughout this deal, far, far more than a trade deal.
In fact, in this deal we find an integration with the United States which, over the next 20 years, will tie us so completely into United States society and United States assumptions that we will not have the ability to shape ourselves a Canadian direction for the future. That is what it is all about.
The Government says that it has been successful in signing this deal. When we actually get out on the hustings and face an election, this deal will be seen by the people of Canada not as a successful deal but as the largest failure of this Government, the failure that does not except us from the omnibus trade Bill in the United States with its various taxes on the capacity of Canadian exporters to export into the United States.
The committee on which I was a member said that we should not sign this deal if the omnibus trade Bill goes through. Last week, the omnibus trade Bill was signed by the President of the United States. It is now law. Yet this Government has not been prepared to withdraw this Bill as the committee suggested.
The Government did not get the exemption which it said was crucial, the exemption from countervail laws. We were told again and again by business people that they had to have that exemption in order to make certain that they had guaranteed access to the United States market. Well, they did not get it. There was no exemption from countervail or from anti-dumping. There was a complete failure on that level.
There was also a failure with respect to subsidies. The Government said that there had to be an agreement on subsidies. Looking through this Bill carefully, we do not find an exemption from subsidies, a code which gathers together an agreement with respect to subsidies. The Government failed at that and it concedes its failure.

They were opposed to a free trade agreement with the United States. When they were running for the leadership of the Progressive Conservative Party, they declared that such a policy was simplistic. A good example is when the Government, in 1985, came out with its very brave Baie Comeau policy with respect to book publishing. According to the trade agreement, now the Canadian Government has the onus put upon it to ensure that there will be fair market price paid to the foreign buyer of this Canadian outfit. It does not say how the fair market price will be determined. The Canadian Government becomes the buyer of last resort.

The Uruguay Round on the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade is studying services. It is looking at the whole element of bringing barriers to services between countries down. Thus what the Hon. Member is saying is only inconsistent within himself. The New Democratic Party's view is to favour the GATT relationships around the world. GATT is the very agency that at this time is studying the removal of barriers on services, not between two countries on a bilateral basis but between many countries on a multilateral basis.
I say to members of the NDP: You cannot have it all ways. That Party is basically trying to proclaim that this agreement fits all the old arguments that its Members used more than 20 years ago when they opposed the Auto Pact, as well as when they opposed the Auto Pact amendments in the early 1970s. When this agreement was coming forward, they suddenly stood up in unison as a Party and with one arm straight in the air said: "Don't you dare touch the Auto Pact". They now use the same elements of argument to try to make Canadians believe that this relationship that will secure our markets, our economy and our jobs has the same evils that they imagined some 20 years ago. They were wrong then and they are wrong today.

Mr. Speaker, as we count the cost of the Saint-Basile-le-Grand tragedy and considering the serious irregularities that have come to light,
we must admit that governments have to take their share of responsibility for this situation.
Mr. Speaker, how does one explain that this warehouse had not been inspected in the past 15 months? Mr. Speaker, the people have the right to know and Governments have the obligation to respond.

 Fort Garry reads as follows:

Mr. Speaker, I rise to speak on this very important amendment. I am very concerned about the fact that the so-called child care strategy brought to the House is one that eliminates people who normally would be able to have some access to child care.
I must say the people, certainly the children, and the families of Canada, are very fortunate that they have had a Member of Parliament such as the Hon. Member for Vancouver East (Ms. Mitchell) who really understands child care. I am very concerned about a Government that will bring forward a Bill that states that this is a child care strategy. What it is really doing is demeaning the ability to deliver child care in our country.
Anyone who has children would start to understand that, first of all, we are looking at children in need and we are looking at children of low-income families who, if the provinces use this Bill, will be cut off in the Canada Assistance Plan. That is really important. We have looked at the statistics and the analysis. We recognize that if the Canada Assistance Plan was left in place at least these people would have access to the kind of quality care that is available to them at the moment.
Second, what we have done with this is said to people who already have spaces, regardless of what kind of spaces they have, that they will be able to get tax exemptions. That is not what we are looking for. We are looking at two million children out there in need of care. Certainly the New Democratic Party has recognized for a long time that to make sure families are secure and have a basis of choice they must have the services that are there. Suggesting that this is something that we cannot afford in Canada is saying that we cannot afford to give stability and caring to families and children. That is not the position of New Democratic Party.
In the Minister's comments yesterday he stated that he was not going to implement the Meech Lake principles. This Government said that it was at last going to be able to establish national standards, but he did not want to do this for children. Again it is this flop-flop that the Government is using. Children are not important to the Government. It is about time that it recognized that the people of Canada do care about their children.
We are looking at a program that will cut off the Canada Assistance Plan that now is at least addressing the needs of low-income people. That plan will be cut off if they kick into this type of Act. That is unacceptable, it is unfair, and it certainly does not serve the children of Canada well.
Canada Child Care Act
There are many research institutions in this country and a lot of research has been done on child development. We have the information, and we know what is needed. We know that those first eight years are the most crucial years in any person's developmental stages, yet the Government is again saying that it is not going to worry about it. Every research institute that looked at child care has said "eliminate the welfare system network for child care and put it into a national child care strategy so all children will be seen as equals, at least for those first eight years". No matter what they have to face in life later on, at least they will be given that base.
What the Government has done in putting this Act in place is discriminating against the low-income people and the people who normally would be able to be part of that welfare assistance plan. The research institutes and the New Democratic Party have stated that if we are going to put a national strategy in place, get that national strategy in place. In the meantime there has to be a phasing in so that the low-income people and the children in real need have the ability to use that Canada Assistance Plan.
This Government has turned down two amendments that would have helped to be put that in place. We have an amendment in front of us this morning that is really saying "allow that to happen", Mr. Speaker, to assist the children who are homeless, the children who are of the working poor, and the families that are under pressure in their existence because of poverty.
It is all very well for the Government to brag about the kinds of programs it has put in place that have actually given assistance to those who already have money, who have places for their child care, and who are comfortable when they go to work knowing that their children are well looked after and that they can afford to pay for it. Is that the kind of society this Government wants to be part of, a society that builds two Canadas, a Canada for the children of those who have the ability to be able to pay for their child care, independent of any help from society, except extra tax exemptions? Rather, do we want to a build a society that says a child born in this country is a valuable treasure, a person that we understand has the potential of being a very productive and secure and creative individual in our country?
As a Party we know that investing in children is probably the most serious and important investment we can make in all times. As New Democrats we understand that if we are going to build a base of a secure society we must build that base in the first eight years of a child's life. If we want families to be able to operate with some security, with knowing that they can build their family unity together with a sense of security that their children will be well looked after and safe, then we need a child care program that does not discriminate against the children in need.

Of the 243,545 licensed day care spaces in Canada in 1987, some 90,386 were in so-called commercial centres or private centres. Of those 90,386, 54,000 of them or 60 per cent were subsidized spaces. This is not something new that is suddenly coming on the scene. The Government is not creating some sort of sinister plot to destroy day care and to destroy the whole system or to change things in a cruel and vicious manner. This is just carrying on the system that has been there for years and years.
If we listen to the comments of the Opposition and what they are suggesting and take them to their logical conclusion that somehow or other we have to wipe out those 90,386 private spaces, wipe out the 54,000 subsidized spaces in those private centres, and start from scratch with non-profit ones, it does not make any sense at all. If what we are interested in is providing day care for families that need it, then there is no point in wiping out what is there and having to replace it with something else. We should all bear these points in mind when we are dealing with this Bill.
Finally, I think that we should bear in mind that there is no provision for capital funding whatsoever under the Canada Assistance Plan. There is in this Bill-and it is one of the big improvements provided by this Bill and by this national child care legislative package-capital funding to allow more day care centres to be built, to allow them to provide extra spaces than there are now, and to provide extra subsidized spaces than there are now. That is what we are talking about, in fact doubling those numbers of subsidized spaces. That is the important and significant. That is why this Bill is so important to our country, as far as I am concerned. It is important to Canadians.
Thousands and thousands of people need day care. They cannot afford to pay for the whole thing themselves. They need some assistance and help if they are going to be working. Many, many single mothers, single parents, if they are going to be working and off the welfare and social assistance rolls, need some sort of subsidized day care space to allow them to do that. I think it is in the national interest to make sure that everybody who wants to work and does not want to be on social assistance has that opportunity. This legislation is geared to that very thing.
Most definitely, the impression that the Opposition has been leaving is that it will not meet that need. In fact, in the next seven years this legislation will double the number of subsidized day care spaces in Canada, and that is something for which the Government and the Minister should be commended.

He said: Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to say a few words on the motion, because it is topical and because it follows the decision taken by this House some time ago, when adopting a new Official Languages Act, in which Section 8 provides that any document tabled in this House by a federal institution, whether the Canadian Government or an agency, shall be tabled in both official languages at the same time.
That section of Bill C-72 reads as follows: Any document made by or under the authority of a federal institution that is tabled in the Senate or the House of Commons by the Government of Canada shall be tabled in both official languages.
As I see it, Mr. Speaker, the point is that the House of Commons is responsible for its own Standing Orders and they must be amended by the House. It does not matter how many Bills we pass, the House has to make a decision and a provision such as the one suggested today must be added to the Standing Orders. This is why the second paragraph states that the Clerk of the House be authorized to print a revised edition of the Standing Orders incorporating the said amendment.
Mr. Speaker, the purpose of my motion is quite simple. Hon. Members will recall that the 1969 legislation had a provision which was the source of some difficulties. Here is the text of section 2 of the Bill adopted in 1969, Chapter 0-2 of the Revised Statutes of Canada: "The English and French languages are the official languages of Canada for all purposes of the Parliament and Government of Canada, and possess and enjoy equality of status and equal rights and privileges as to their use in all the institutions of the Parliament and Government of Canada." That is clear enough: English and French are the official languages of Canada for all purposes of the Parliament and Government of Canada.
Up until 1987-88 my personal experience has been that the Government always tabled official documents in both official languages. As a rule, parliamentary institutions and government agencies did follow this instruction and documents were tabled in both official languages.

Speech:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to add my support to the amendments which we are discussing and to urge the Minister to accept them.


I note, and put on the record as I think others have done, the views of the President of Knowledge Network, Mr. Glenn Farrell, who said in respect of this Bill:
The amendments to Bill C-136, proposed by federal Communications Minister Flora MacDonald are inadequate because they fail to recognize the important role that educational broadcasters play in Canada. This Bill downgrades the role of educational broadcasters at a time when regional communications are increasingly important.
There is not a Member of Parliament who has young children or young grandchildren, as 1 do, who cannot help but realize how much more knowledge our young people between the ages of four and eight or four and ten have about matters than children had 10 or 20 years ago. This is so because they have the opportunity to watch educational programs like Sesame Street and many others too numerous for me to report on. Any Bill which does not expand the ability of TV to disseminate more and more educational programming is deficient.
I want to speak about another aspect of the Bill, dealing not just with children. For almost as many years as I have been a Member of Parliament, I have raised questions about the fact that 20 per cent of the people of Canada are functionally illiterate, this at a time when we know that businesses, industries and farmers are facing increasing competition, making it tougher and tougher to be a success. Other countries have moved ahead of us because of their knowledge and ability to use the newest technology. How could the 20 per cent of Canadians who are functionally illiterate possibly find jobs, even if we lived in a period of full employment in that future when they do not have the ability to fill the jobs which are or will be available.
In the 1984 Throne Speech of the Government was a promise that dealing with illiteracy was to be a major objective of this Conservative Government. Silnce then virtually nothing was done by the federal Government, much too little is being done by the provincial Governments, and the voluntary organizations working in the field do not have the financial ability to do the job they want and need to do.
Four years have gone by and suddenly, two weeks ago, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) resurrected this important question, which he ignored for four years, and announced that the Government is proposing to spend over $100 million in the next four years dealing with illiteracy. We know that 20 per cent of the people of Canada are functionally illiterate, but nobody has any real information on the numbers of people who are attending programs organized by the provincial Governments and by volunteer organizations such as Frontier College or one such as that just started less than a year ago with offices in the constituency of my colleague, the Hon. Member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Keeper), called Beat the Street.
Nobody knows how many people are in the programs. As a matter of fact one of the little tasks I have set for my staff is to get in touch with every such organization across Canada to
Broadcasting Act
find out how many people are in these programs. I have some idea of the information they will get. We will find that probably fewer than 5 per cent of the five million people who are functionally illiterate are in programs that will help them.
My colleague, the Hon. Member from Hamilton, has talked about the problems of native people. In cities like Winnipeg, Regina or Vancouver, to mention just three, one cannot help, if one drives around these cities, but note the tremendous movement into the cities of native people from the reserves. They come to the cities and their ability to speak English is far from what it should be. Many of them are in fact functionally illiterate.
In these cities, there is a time bomb which is ticking away and which will explode. Dealing with illiteracy is just one of the questions that we have to address if that time bomb is in fact not to explode. One of the ways it can be dealt with is by giving the broadcasting system, radio and television stations, public and private, not only the right to put on educational programs but the resources to do the job. Perhaps, for the private sector, we need legislation which will force the broadcasters to do some of the educational and cultural things they promised to do when they got their licences and which in fact they almost completely ignored once they were successful in getting the licenses. What they have concentrated on is having the right, as I think the Caplan-Sauvageau Commission has pointed out, to virtually to print money and make tremendous profits in return on their investment.
This is the situation we are in. It is a very desperate situation, it is a very serious situation. It is a situation which needs to be dealt with in every possible way. One of the ways is to amend this Bill so that the Broadcasting Act will make it very clear that radio and television stations and the networks have the right, and I would say the responsibility, to increase and improve educational programming. We need this amendment in the Bill.

Madam Speaker, it is an honour and privilege to rise on Motion M-151 to put to the House and Canadians an idea that I believe is essential to the future and the long-term stability of our country as a nation and as a society.
The basic principle of the motion requires a constitutional amendment that would require governments to balance the budgets we present here in Parliament. I have listed three exceptions. One is a declared national emergency. Another is a declared national disaster. The third is if this Parliament, by a vote of two-thirds of its Members, declares in favour of a deficit. I hasten to reassure Members that I am not wedded to the specific wording of the basic principle or the exceptions. There may well be other exceptions that Members come up with that we would all find acceptable. Perhaps a two-thirds majority is too high. However, it seems to me as parliamentarians our prime concern has to be for the long-term future and stability of our country.
We entrench in our Constitution our democratic rights because we know we cannot trust power solely to people. We also entrench human rights. I certainly would be prepared to work with other Members to work up a constitutional amendment that would protect future generations from environmental breaches. We need environmental protection in our Constitution for future generations. However, the purpose of this debate is constitutional protection for future generations on economic matters.
Why am I concerned? This year the deficit will be some $28 billion. Members know that a mere four years ago it was $38 billion. Certainly it is being reduced each year and that is a step in the right direction, but on April 1 of every year the deficit is moved over to the national debt. Members will remember that in 1968 the national debt was some $18 billion, even though we had built this country, fought two world wars, and endured 10 years of depression. However, since 1968, as a result of succeeding government budget deficits, the national debt has gone up to over $300 billion. The cost of servicing that debt is something like $31 billion or $32 billion. That is at current interest rates. We remember that three short years ago interest rates were 23 per cent. That would mean over $60 billion coming right off the top just to service the debt. I firmly believe that would lead to instability and rash action which could impair the future of our country. Certainly it would affect the well being of future generations.
As you well know, the national debt is simply excess spending on ourselves. Yet it has to be paid for by someone. If we do not, it will be put off into the future and our children and grandchildren will pay it. That will be done either through increased taxes or they will receive far fewer services. Or, some future Government will simply turn on the printing presses and we know what that does. We just need to look at all the Third World countries which have a small group of people who are fabulously rich and a mass of poor people. When you look at their economic history, every one has had a government which turned on the printing press and paid their national debt in that way. However, that leads to inflation, high interest rates and collapse. Surely none of us would individually impose that on our children or our grandchildren. Yet collectively since 1968 we have run our national debt from $18 billion to over $300 billion.


What I am saying, and I would like to hear other Members' views, is that it has got so bad that we now need a constitutional amendment that will protect our children and grandchildren from us. That is a terrible thing to say, but the fact is that representative parliamentary democracy has developed to the point in this country and others, particularly in the western world, where the interest groups are so powerful that they are able to convince Parliament to override the broad general interest of the country as a whole. Madam Speaker, I thank the Hon. Member for the question. I was much taken with the preamble to his question in which he cited the tremendous impact upon Canadian culture of the American media. I immediately began to reflect upon that most conspicuous of matters treated in recent weeks by the American media, to wit, the presidential election. I like to think of Canada as a tolerant country, a country that accepts dissent, accepts a diversity of opinion. Indeed, I would like to think of Canada as-and please do not misunderstand me, let me make sure that I say this clearly- essentially a small "1" liberal country. I mean that to construe a nation of tolerance, of diversity of ideas and dissent.
We are being bombarded with the notion that somehow it is a sin to be a liberal by an American media which, through this Bill will gain, one way or another, continued and perhaps expanded access to Canada as an audience. It is suggested that to believe seriously that sticking laser weapons and other kinds of contraptions in orbit for war purposes is destabilizing, and to describe it as such and to suggest for a moment that these mass expenditures on weapons constitute a danger to society is somehow bad. They suggest that if every American does not, at every excuse, jump up and recite the Pledge of Allegiance, that is somehow un-American.
I know, Madam Speaker, that just as I and my colleague from Vancouver-Kingsway, you have been aware of what is going on there. That is an election that is based on the notion that a good society is an intolerant society. This may seem like a small thing but I think that most Canadians, were they to realize that this pervasive encroachment of the American media and those kinds of American attitudes have a serious impact on our young people, would be offended by it if they examined it for just a moment.
Surely it is significant to our country that those attitudes, which have developed in another nation with a history quite different from ours, should become determinant in our own
Broadcasting Act
attitudes in a country which I consider to be one of the more civilized countries in the world. Inevitably, if we do not enhance the opportunity for Canadians to have greater and greater access to those attitudes which are the foundation of our nation, our nation will be threatened seriously.
I find it offensive to have a trade deal that says that if we attempt to increase the degree to which we communicate our values through our cultural media there will be retaliation from our trading partner, the partner in the economic agreement. That, all by itself, is sufficient reason for rejecting the trade deal.
I do not know whether, in expressing this concern, I have specifically answered the question of my respected colleague, but I thank him for the opportunity to allow me to point out the real impact that the present debate in the United States has on our country through the American media. More important, the content of that debate is so destructive, so pitiful in its disregard even for American values, that I fear the penetration of such a set of values in our own country. Without any means of limiting it, it promises difficulties for us in the future.
